Why Civic Interplay
Information may be abundant. Legibility is not.
But that can change.
Many conversations about AI focus on automation and its impacts, positive and negative.
Civic Interplay takes a different approach. It asks: What can be learned about communities in transition, using agent-based tools for discovery and collaboration?
By interpreting public records for public conversation, Civic Interplay contributes to the growing field of 'civic AI'. It tests and evaluates how AI can support civic empowerment in places and communities, and build community trust in public institutions.

Title: A side angle on place flows
Project: Tracing public value: A side angle on a place
Contents:
Civic Interplay · experimental
A side angle on place flows
This project is entirely speculative, using indicative data only.
The point is to visualise how the value of a precinct over time might start to be visualised through its historical public registers of investment flows, considered against its named priorities and targets.
In this instance, the visualisation considers a 20-year time span of public commitments to increased tree canopy targets. It points to the idea that proposed versus actual spending can be mapped at localised level, using easily-accessible tools and prompts using openly available data (government open data, annual or statutory reports, local ecology maps).
If making a tool like this is no longer hard, what kinds of uses might records like this have? For example, could different beneficiaries of investment in street trees contribute over time, helping to annotate and share the value they receive? How might be these less traditional sources of ‘data’, expressed as nature regeneration or care, be made more visible alongside public records?
Study: urban forest under densificationIllustrative layout and figures, not real dataDrag the timeline below to move through the record
2026The record to date
1Misalignment
Value and flows. People asked for shade on the walk to school. In that part of the precinct the flows are development approvals, and the planting money went elsewhere. The ground shows it: sparse canopy where shade was asked for.
2Accountability
Flows and impact. An approval was granted on conditions about trees. The line drops from the permit and stops, because nothing in the public record says whether the conditions were met.
3Illegibility
Value and impact. People wrote letters to trees. That attachment is real and it matters, but there is no field anywhere to hold it, so the line never reaches the ground. The empty outline is drawn on purpose.

Title: An infrastructural-AI stack
Contents:
Civic Interplay / Field note
An infrastructural-AI stack
An AI system is not one thing. It is a stack of six layers, and different people own each one. This is what that looks like in Australia, from the minerals in the ground to where the profit is finally booked.
Field note, 16 August 2026. The full-size card as published.
06 Value & returns Booked through Dublin and Singapore. Paused on tax, conditioned on copyright. Who holds it Offshore
05 Models & workloads Foreign weights running on leased capacity. No instrument asks who the compute serves. Who holds it US labs
04 Compute The public share is roughly 150 H100-equivalents, about A$70 million. Research allocation is oversubscribed threefold. Who holds it Hyperscalers
03 Facilities A$65 billion of announced private build. Blackstone, AWS, Microsoft, Google (paused). Who holds it Global funds
02 Land, water, energy Granted through state planning. Fast-tracked, with public notice exempted. Who holds it Australia
01 Minerals Scandium and rare earths. A Pentagon loan, Lockheed holding first offer, and China refining around 90 per cent. Who holds it Washington / Beijing
The short version
Three vertical integrators, and one horizontal middle. Australia holds the ground that the stack is built on, and almost nothing above it. The layer granted through state planning is the layer where public notice is exempted, which means the one part of the stack under Australian control is also the part decided with the least public involvement.
Read the stack from the bottom up and it is a story about resources. Read it from the top down and it is a story about where the returns go. Both readings end in the same middle, and that middle is the only place a state government currently has leverage.
Figures are drawn from press reporting. Verify before citation. If you find an error, the correction form below goes straight into the tracker.
What to do with this
The useful question is not who is to blame, it is where the leverage sits. Layer 02 is the answer, because it is the layer a state or local government actually decides. The companion field note sets out what could be asked for at that point of decision.

Title: The local benefit ladder
Contents:
Civic Interplay / Field note
What could a community actually ask for?
When a data centre is proposed nearby, the conversation usually stops at jobs and rates. This is a longer list. Eight rungs, running from compensation at the bottom to co-ownership at the top, and every one of them names a mechanism that already works somewhere in the world.
Field note. The annotated version, showing where each rung is drawn from, is set out in full below.
08 Standing A consultative committee with review triggers, so the community has a seat that persists after approval. Drawn from Community Consultative Committee NSW Planning (DPHI), major-project planning
07 Community benefit fund A host fee paid into a local fund, on the model already used for benefit-sharing. Drawn from Benefit-sharing payment, $1,050 per MW per year EnergyCo NSW, renewable energy zones
06 Equity participation A community stake in the facility itself, through co-investment rather than compensation. Drawn from Co-ownership models (Power in Partnership) Community Power Agency, community energy
05 Heat and grid services Waste heat recovered and sold on, plus offtake and energy buffering back to the grid. Drawn from Waste-heat offtake to district grid Stockholm Exergi, district heating
04 Data sovereignty Consented use, data residency, and a data trust governing what the facility may hold. Drawn from Kaitiakitanga data licence Te Hiku Media, Aotearoa New Zealand
03 Inference access Public-interest inference endpoints, so local institutions can actually use the compute. Drawn from AI Factories access commitment EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, public AI Adjacent precedent, verify before use
02 Managed access An allocator, plus the skills and technical support to make an allocation usable. Drawn from National Merit Allocation Scheme NCI, ANU, research computing Adjacent precedent, verify before use
01 Reserved capacity Compute reserved for local use, counted in GPU-hours. Drawn from Domestic Gas Reservation Policy WA Government, gas and resources
Why a ladder
A ladder rather than a list, because the rungs are not equivalent. The bottom of the ladder is compensation: something given in exchange for accepting the facility. The top is co-ownership: a share in what the facility is and does. Most negotiations never leave the bottom rung, and often not even all of it.
Only a partial share of rung 01 exists in Australia today. Everything above it is drawn from somewhere else, which is the point. None of this is invented. It is a matter of applying instruments that already exist in energy, in resources, in research computing and in Indigenous data governance to a kind of infrastructure that has so far escaped them.
Two rungs are marked as adjacent precedent. They are close analogues rather than direct ones, so the framing needs checking before it goes to a state government. The other six are in force somewhere today.
Using it
The ladder is most useful as a checklist in a room. When a proposal is on the table, work up from rung 01 and ask which rungs are being offered, which are being refused, and on what grounds. A refusal at rung 07 is a different conversation from a refusal at rung 02, and naming which rung you are on tends to move a negotiation faster than arguing in general terms.
It also pairs with the stack. The stack shows where the leverage sits, at the land, water and energy layer that a state or local government decides. The ladder is what to ask for once you are standing there.

Title: About
Contents:
About
About Civic Interplay
Major transformations are reshaping places and communities, from the energy, water and data infrastructure being built, to the pressures on environments and habitats in a heating world.
Civic Interplay links critical enquiry and community partnerships with AI tools. Most of the work involves assembling and interpreting published records on how places are changing, to improve community knowledge and information transparency.
The project contributes to a growing field of practice known as ‘civic AI’, which considers AI adoption both for civic empowerment and for building community trust in public institutions.
It is designed as a testing ground for active experimentation, where results are made available to inform public conversation, and to invite active collaborations.
Can we use AI tools to make the transitions shaping communities and places more visible?

MethodGathering Intelligences
Tools & experiments
Open experimentation
This is a methodology that is in development, which means that experimentation is deliberately open. Not everything will be successful; perhaps some tools and ideas will be mistakes. The purpose behind this is to build a greater sense of agency among those who may feel excluded from decisions about how value is being captured and shared within their communities.
While transparency is never an end in itself, the methods here seek to bring attention to the important role that everyday digital capabilities play in shaping civic agency, towards more effective governance.
On the use of AI
Agents and AI workflows are key to the civic interplay method. Agentic workflows are tested and trialled, in order to read and interrogate information records that are publicly available. This includes open government data and other information that is available via the public web. By diving in, these methods also establish practices of critical enquiry and sense-checking around the adoption of agents as effective co-enquirers. This practice also experimentally seeks to understand where the new forms of ‘data enclosure’ exist or are emerging, in the way that previous platform ecosystems built the moats around their intelligence.
AI is used to gather and read record. The interpretation and judgement remain human, along with the prose.

Title: Gathering Intelligences
Contents:
Experimental method
Gathering Intelligences
Four steps for reading how flows of value have shaped a place.
A journey of enquiry
EnquiryStart with a question, not an answer.
LiteracyBeing able to read a place for yourself: who made a record, why, and what it leaves out.
LegibilityInformation that was hidden or unreadable becomes accessible and more legible to others.
AgencyThe journey of enquiry aims to inform communities around how decisions are made, and according to what values.
Step 1
Assemble the records
Gather what is already on the public record about a project or precinct, through time.
Choose a place with edges: a precinct, a corridor, a project. Then find where its records live: strategies and masterplans, planning approvals, budgets and grant registers, environment effects statements, canopy and other surveys, submissions and media statements.
This is where civic AI helps. Agents can assemble far more of the public record than one person could, and set it out in date order. Each record keeps a link to its source, so anyone can check it.
Where do the records for this place live?
Who made each one, and whose interests does it serve?
What is missing, and since when?
Start assembling
Step 2
Begin your dig
What was the core priority for your place twenty years ago? Or ten?
Start to explore what the key care factors were that have shaped flows of investment over time. Read each priority in the context of its moment: the rules, pressures and promises that produced it.
Then trace what followed: what was approved, what was funded, what was built, and what quietly lapsed.
What did the plan say mattered, and when?
Where did the money and approvals go after that?
Which commitments have no record of what happened next?
Begin your dig
Step 3
Making sense
What might be the most useful ways to interpret what you have assembled?
Discuss it with others. Would it read best as a map, a diagram, or a chart? Each shows something different: a map shows where, a diagram shows how things connect, a chart shows change over time.
Then look across the whole record. Which values are most evident in the data you assembled, and which are hard to find?
A map, a diagram, or a chart?
What values are most evident in the data you assembled?
Which values are hardest to see?
See examples
Step 4
Sense checking
Visit your place, and contribute to the terrain.
Go for a walk and examine the ground. Some of what matters about a place has never been written down; noticing it is part of the reading.
Then bring the two together: how does your walk relate to what you assembled?
How does your walk and your data assembling relate?
Can you see connections between the two?
What is worth bringing back to your digital resource?

Title: A video player that doesn't watch you back
Contents:
The player
A video player that doesn't watch you back
This is a draft. A small video player, built as a counter-model.
Most embedded players are surveillance instruments wearing a play button. They set cookies, load third-party scripts, log who watched what and for how long, and feed it back into a recommendation machine you don't control. Until recently this one quietly did some of that too: it pulled its typeface from Google's servers, so every viewer's browser phoned home before the video even started. We noticed. We fixed it.
Now it doesn't. The media sits on our own storage. There are no third-party scripts, no cookies, no tracking pixels, no algorithm deciding what you see next. If Civic Interplay disappeared tomorrow, the file would still play and you could still download it.
It is a tiny thing. But sovereignty over infrastructure starts with small refusals: the choice to host your own file, to not phone home, to let a viewer just watch.
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Christopher Olah at the Vatican, May 2026. Civic Interplay
The promises
No third-party scripts, no cookies. The player calls no domain but our own. Nothing to consent to.
Self-hosted media. The video files live on our storage, not a platform's.
Captioned and legible by default. Accessibility is the baseline, not an add-on.
Portable. Native, downloadable, and it keeps working if we don't.
Put it on your own site
Paste this wherever you can drop HTML. It loads nothing from us until someone presses play.

Title: The proposition
Contents:
About
The proposition
The conditions of AI governance have traditionally been the domain of technical and policy experts, not citizens or placemakers. Yet increasingly, the way a place is made legible to its community is through digital knowledge systems that foster particular ways of seeing the world, and each other.
What happens when these interfaces become extractive surveillance platforms, or bring large-scale data centres into a community to compete for scarce natural resources? Growing conflicts over digital infrastructure in an era of AI point to a breakdown in community trust: in how that infrastructure is governed, and in what it means for a community's wellbeing.
In the context of AI services and systems, governing digital infrastructure well, under democratic conditions, depends on greater legibility and accountability to place-based communities.
To this end, Civic Interplay explores what practices and forums promote greater transparency and legibility around how digital and data ecosystems shape places.
What forms of civic enquiry are possible in an era of AI infrastructure?
When digital infrastructure shapes the material and ecological logics of places more explicitly, what forms of democratic accountability do communities expect, and what are they able to access?
Information is abundant. Legibility is unevenly distributed.
Why now
Open data to platform technology to infrastructural AI to civic enquiry
1Open data
The open data movement was built on the premise that data transparency would lead to greater accountability. Governments published, and the public record became more readable than ever.
2Platform technology
Instead, much of that open data fed platform technologies that built closed data ecosystems on it, and on the data people gave them, behind hidden algorithms and paywalls. Legibility gathered with the platforms, not the public.
3Infrastructural AI
Frontier AI models have since absorbed public data at far greater scale. The paywall is different, a subscription rather than a lock, and the tools they enable are far more abundant. The infrastructure behind them, including data centres arriving in communities, is governed in ways that are harder to see.
4Civic enquiry
Where trust in how digital infrastructure is governed is breaking down, Civic Interplay builds on what open data investment created, and asks what becomes possible when active citizens enlist AI agents in acts of civic enquiry. The aim is to move data-driven enquiry beyond specialist knowledge, towards everyday knowledge practices, citizen sensing and open forums, and to seek shared benefits from digital infrastructure in more accountable ways.

Title: Data Centres Transparency Project
Contents:
Civic Interplay / Tracker
Data Centres Transparency Project
A living atlas of infrastructural AI in Australia. Site by site, it records who owns the compute, what each facility draws in power and water, how it was approved, where it has been contested, and which supply chains it depends on. The tracker is open: the code base is on GitHub, alongside summary data sheets for each State and Territory, a glossary, a methods statement and a news feed (RSS).
Data Centres Transparency Project
Open the map in a new tab
If the map does not load, your browser may be blocking the embedded site. Open it in a new tab instead.
This project examines data centre approvals in Australia as a contested terrain, reflecting competing versions of agency and sovereignty that are expressed by place-based communities.
The tracker is the first practice-based methodological expansion of civic AI by researcher and digital strategist Dr Sarah Barns (RMIT University). It uses AI skills and methods to make flows of public value more accountable and legible, while also examining the extent to which current practices of data governance support the goals of transparency and democratic accountability.
A core proposition being tested here is that digital tools, including AI agents, can be used to expand and democratise how public policies are understood and interpreted for their impacts on places over time.
However, their effectiveness also depends on a set of core digital capabilities and services that require concurrent investment for this methodology to be practical and meaningful. These include: open and machine-readable data infrastructures, commitment to open and transparent reporting around public value and accountability, and digital literacies around platform dependencies and their consequences for digital agency, including AI agency.
Civic AI applied to data centre approvals
Combined with a place-based approach, the tools of civic AI are being adopted to interrogate how public policy frameworks are adapting to a ‘super cycle’ wave of infrastructural AI investment in Australia.
Key focus areas for this Data Centre Tracker include:
comparative levels of data transparency across states and territories;
forms of governance practised in the approvals process;
levels of data transparency relative to purported claims; and
expressions of civic agency evidenced through the formal public approvals process.
The methodology operates as a form of recursive listening, where sites of urban transformation are read as informational archives, structured and interpreted through distinctive methods for listening, attention, interpretation and gathering over time (including information gathering).
Attention to this dimension of urban transformation is designed to foster greater awareness of the role and value of informational transparency and accountability in shaping good governance and decision making on behalf of current and future generations.
Mapping AI sovereignties
Core to this tracker is the recognition that AI sovereignty is mobilised as a highly normative term that supports the accumulation of value, public and private, around investment in AI infrastructure globally.
However, AI sovereignty as a framework mobilised to support investment in AI infrastructure and skills also operates to undermine existing practices of sovereignty, including place-based sovereignties: Country-centred and local community sovereignties.
Negotiations over contested versions of sovereignty occur at the site of data centre approvals, where local and state-based planning regimes approve large-scale data centres supported by vast global investment flows, as well as national sovereignty actors in the form of sovereign wealth funds and superannuation funds.
National policies also advance national sovereignty goals for digital infrastructure through public policy settings including, in Australia, the Foreign Investment Review Board (FIRB) and spending on public compute.
Each of these layers reflects different values towards the nature of digital sovereignty, and in particular AI sovereignty, and each is a focus for this tracker.
Global news coverage mentioning “sovereign AI” or “AI sovereignty”, relative volume, 2022 to 2026. Source: GDELT. Data and method in the project explainer.
Key findings and methods
In Australia, dependency on global cloud providers is a condition of participation in AI infrastructure. This is reflected in the reliance on the US frontier model developer Anthropic in the development of this civic AI methodology (noting that alternative models are also available).
Tracking the approvals of data centres in Australia (view the map), the project identifies key trends in both approvals and data transparency, alongside summary data sheets by state and territory and news reportage, and the full contestation record in Notion. A summary of the methodology adopted for the project is below, with an accompanying glossary of key terms, the fact-checking protocol used for human verification, a GitHub repository and a DOI for citation purposes.
Every box is marked as done by a person or by an AI agent. Download the diagram (SVG)
Platform dependencies
The tracker depends on parts of the stack it maps, and it records that dependency.
Anthropic. Claude is the model behind the research agents. Sites in the tracker listed as hosting, or planned to host, Anthropic’s models in Australia include AWS Asia Pacific (Sydney), Amazon’s Sydney and Melbourne investment, Google Cloud Sydney and Melbourne, and the proposed Western Downs Digital Park near Dalby (lease subject to FIRB approval).
Notion holds the database. All data can be exported at any time.
MCP and public APIs connect the tools.
Cloudflare and Mapbox provide hosting and base maps.
Factiva provides licensed news through an RMIT licence. It is read by hand, never scraped.
GitHub holds the code, data and documentation. Each version is deposited on Zenodo with a DOI.
Accounting for compute costs
The project also runs a tracker of the reported computational costs of the research, in the Cost of Compute tracker, and the same records are saved in the GitHub repository.

Title: Submission to the Senate Inquiry into AI and Data Centres
Contents:
Civic Interplay / Submission
Submission to the Senate Inquiry into AI and Data Centres
Submission to the Senate Environment and Communications References Committee inquiry into Artificial Intelligence and Data Centres, lodged 1 September 2026. It draws on the Data Centres Transparency Project, and makes fourteen recommendations.
Lead author
Dr Sarah Barns
Contributing authors
Dr Kajsa Lundberg, Dr Emma McRae, Associate Professor Ascelin Gordon
Prepared at
Centre for Urban Research, RMIT University
Lodged
1 September 2026
Read the full submission See the Tracker
What this submission argues
Australia's digital infrastructure is foundational to its national sovereignty. It is a strength of Australian democracy that an investment wave of this scale can be brought into the public realm for contestation and debate; such debate is itself part of the critical infrastructure of Australian democracy. Sovereignty should not be pursued at the expense of the democratic conditions for accountability and transparency that Australia as a nation helped to pioneer.
The current debate has also revealed how little visibility communities have into which level of government makes the decisions that shape their lives, a gap that opaque approval pathways widen. Many of the critical decisions shaping data centre infrastructure are being made through fast-track planning pathways that exempt or truncate community consultation and public exhibition, without transparency around environmental impacts. This heightens environmental, social and economic risks, and investors are already expressing concern that data centres are losing their social licence to operate.
Core to our submission is therefore the need for greater transparency in the planning and approval of data centres across all levels of government, and ongoing monitoring against approved resource impacts to ensure they do not contravene existing sovereign commitments.
It is not acceptable, in an era of information abundance, that such long-lived and resource-intensive assets can be approved without public exhibition. Much of this lies with state planning regimes, but the Commonwealth should use its powers to advance national standards and mandatory national reporting. Investment in sovereign digital infrastructure should not undermine Australia's existing commitments, including its Nationally Determined Contribution under the Paris Agreement and the due diligence obligations recently affirmed by the International Court of Justice.
Nor should this investment be a missed opportunity. Benefit-sharing and precinct-scale innovation districts can strengthen Australia's skills and knowledge ecosystem and accelerate the transition away from the resource dependencies driving global heating. And in advancing Indigenous data sovereignty, consistent with the National AI Plan's commitments and the Framework for Governance of Indigenous Data, Australia can lead the world in recognising the knowledge systems that have nurtured people on this continent for millennia.
From the covering letter to the Committee.
Summary of Key Recommendations
Transparency and disclosure
Mandatory disclosure at application stage
Resource impacts of data centre developments to be mandated for data centres above 5MW. Applicants to state expected electrical load, expected annual water demand by source (potable, recycled, or other), and cooling technology. These disclosures should form part of the publicly exhibited application documents, not commercial-in-confidence annexures available only to agencies.
Public exhibition stage should not be ignored
Fast-track programs such as Victoria's Development Facilitation Program should not extinguish exhibition for facilities of this scale. A minimum public notice and comment window, allowing sufficient time for public engagement and consultation, should apply nationally, incorporated into the national data centre principles flagged in the National AI Plan and consistent with the 'meaningful community consultation' expectation now embedded in the NSW Data Centre Policy Framework.
Support for local government
Referral packages to councils must include load data. Agency assessments of grid and water impacts should also be published alongside any approval outcome.
Monitoring and reporting
A national public register
A national public register of data centre applications and performance, carrying the mandated fields above, with annual reporting of actual consumption against approved estimates on a mandatory NABERS-style basis, to ensure ongoing monitoring over time. Modelled on existing schemes such as the National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting scheme and the NABERS disclosure regime, alongside adjacent amendments to state planning systems.
Transparent reporting on energy sources
Public renewable energy claims by data centre operators should distinguish contracted supply, certificate matching and offsets, consistent with ACCC guidance on environmental claims, and be verifiable against the register. Any claims of renewable supply should demonstrate additionality and be verifiable through REGO time and location matching, with facility registration data reported to AEMO.
Mandatory e-waste and server lifecycle reporting
Data centre operators should be required to report server stock, turnover rates and e-waste recycling outcomes annually through the public register, so that Australia's exposure to AI-driven e-waste growth can be measured and managed before turnover volumes peak.
Demand evidence of environmental impact
Approvals should be conditional on demonstrably additional renewable supply to match demand, no reliance on new or extended fossil generation, and consistency with legislated Commonwealth and state emissions targets, assessed against cumulative demand.
Community benefit and compute access
Benefit sharing agreements
National data centre standards should include a benefit-sharing obligation for facilities above 5MW. Modelled on the per-megawatt community benefit contributions established for renewable energy zone generators in NSW, calculated per megawatt of approved load, indexed, for the operating life of the facility. The obligation should attach to the land through conditions of consent rather than to the corporate applicant, and payments should be reported through the public register.
Compute access as condition of consent
We support the Albanese Government's stated intention to convert Expectation 5 of the Expectations of data centres and AI infrastructure developers to a binding requirement. Compute-access obligations for Australian researchers, small businesses and public institutions should be assessable against a public register.
Sovereignty claims and Commonwealth agreements
Commonwealth facilitation conditional on disclosure
Where the Commonwealth enters memoranda of understanding or comparable arrangements with global AI companies, alignment with the Government's Expectations of data centres and AI infrastructure developers should be evidenced through mandatory disclosures, and the terms of any commitments made, including benefit-sharing and compute-access commitments, should be published in full.
Define sovereign capability by layer
Any claim of sovereign AI capability in a government to company agreement should specify which specific layer of the technology stack it refers to. Domestic hosting of physical infrastructure should not be claimed as equivalent to domestic control of AI capability. Appendix B sets out the dimensions of the 'infrastructural AI stack' for this purpose.
Address gaps in the application of sovereignty to Australia's Indigenous data sovereignty layer
Sovereign capability claims currently attach to compute, facilities and models, while Indigenous data sovereignty remains the only register of sovereignty in the stack with no binding instrument in any approval pathway. Commonwealth agreements with global AI companies, and the national data centre principles flagged in the National AI Plan, should give effect to the Framework for Governance of Indigenous Data (2024) and be consistent with the Maiam nayri Wingara principles and the CARE principles for Indigenous data governance, including through data governance conditions in facilitation agreements and Commonwealth procurement.
National consistency
A pause on approvals until nationally-consistent frameworks apply
New data centre approvals above 5MW should be paused until the nationally consistent standards flagged in the National AI Plan, the National Electricity Rule changes to be considered by the Energy and Climate Change Ministerial Council in September 2026, and the disclosure and benefit-sharing requirements recommended in this submission are in force.
Advance nationally-consistent definitions of land use
The Commonwealth should advocate for nationally-consistent definitions of data centres as a distinct use class in state planning schemes, assessed by reference to megawatts of connected load rather than floor area, and preferentially located within designated precincts that enable heat reuse, recycled water, grid coordination and research co-location, on the model of renewable energy zones.
Key Data Centres Transparency Project findings
As at August 2026.
Of the 69 sites in the analysis subset, 38 were approved through processes with no public exhibition, whether by fast-track designation or under a state significant development pathway. That is 55 per cent.
Capacity figures are publicly available for only 30 of the 69 approvals. In Victoria in 2026, twelve sites were approved with no public exhibition at all.
Across thirteen approved or lodged Victorian applications audited in August 2026, none disclosed expected electricity or water demand, and only one reported its cooling method.
The megawatt figures in public circulation, 162MW at Fishermans Bend, 400MW plus at Laverton North, 354MW at Tullamarine, appear only in corporate press releases and government investment promotion material.
Applications are being lodged by engineering consultants or shelf companies. The 354MW Tullamarine campus was approved in the name of EMKC3 Pty Ltd. The owner, AirTrunk, became known only after approval, through an application to correct the permit.
Data centres consume roughly 3 per cent of national electricity today, projected to reach 13 per cent by 2036.
What the submission addresses
The submission responds to two of the Committee's terms of reference: the effectiveness of existing regulatory frameworks in managing the growth of data centres in Australia, including deals between the Government and global AI companies, and the potential impacts of artificial intelligence and data centres on Australian communities, industries and the environment, including water and energy.
It draws on the Data Centres Transparency Project, established in 2026. As at August 2026 the tracker covered 89 sites, of which 69 informed the analysis. Methods, evidence documents and the fact-checking protocol are published in the project's data repository (doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21994643).
Read the full submission, including the response to each term of reference, the reference list, the civic AI methods appendix and the infrastructural AI stack.
The evidence base is the Data Centres Transparency Project. The background to the project is in Mapping Australian Data Centres.

Title: You, me, data and the city
Contents:
Essay
You, me, data and the city
Is the data-rich city taking on a life of its own? And can Hugh Stretton’s Ideas for Australian Cities help us navigate its hazards? Originally published in 2019.
January 2021
To mark the 50th anniversary of Hugh Stretton’s Ideas for Australian Cities, Inside Story commission me to write a piece on digital technology in Australian cities today. Many thanks to Inside Story, and to CAL, for the opportunity to reflect on the relevance of Stretton’s work to today’s digitally infused urban experiences.
Introductory excerpt below. Full article published at Inside Story.
It’s time to head to the airport. Bag packed, call the cab. Better make it an Uber — at least you know exactly when your car will arrive. And your driver’s behaviour is being graded out of five stars, which I’ve found means the trip is more likely to be convivial. I often find myself deep in conversation with Uber drivers, in a way that’s rare in a taxi. Perhaps we’re both performing for the algorithm, or at least made to feel safer in the knowledge that each of us has a stake in the conversation going well.
I wait seven minutes before the car arrives. My driver this time is Australian-born, and we get chatting pretty quickly. I learn he’s driving Ubers on the side while doing his MBA. While we talk, we also negotiate with the digital map that lurks on the dashboard, giving us instructions on where to go. I have my own favourite routes through the local streets that get me to Sydney’s airport, but the map, fed by data obtained from all of us going about our daily business, has its own ideas. I tell my driver about a photographer friend of mine, also an Uber driver on the side, who likes to run two versions of Google maps when he’s driving, one within the Uber app and one straight from Google. My friend says the Uber route is just slightly longer, and therefore more expensive, most of the time. That seems hard to be believe, my driver told me, but yeah, maybe.
My driver and I get to talking about Uber’s opening up to public shareholders earlier this year, which saw the company attract a lower sharemarket price than was anticipated, mostly because of revelations by the company that it was struggling to make a profit from ride-sharing. My driver was pretty well informed about all this. “For Uber, long term, it’s about the data, not the ride-sharing,” he explained to me, not knowing quite how obsessed I was with the company myself, and with the rise of data-driven urban platforms more generally. I nodded and agreed. Yep, it’s all about the data.
We’d probably been reading similar stories about Uber in the news recently. Dara Khosrowshahi, the chief executive, seems to be running a PR campaign about the company’s ambitions to become the “broker of human movement” — specifically, of “people, food, and freight” — in cities. Kind of like the Amazon of transportation, he has been saying. When it was first launched, Uber created a new marketplace for ride-sharing by better connecting people who needed a lift somewhere with people who could trade some, or most, of their spare time for extra money. Uber Eats, launched in 2012, has likewise provided a simple way for people to order takeaway food, by connecting these people with others in their city who would happily deliver it to them for a small fee without having to be tied to one particular restaurant. Uber Freight is coming too, an app that “matches carriers with shippers” in a way that presumably will aim to beat systems people use now to get their freight where it needs to be.
I wonder aloud, to my driver, what kind of “broker” of human movement Uber is. Is it really so “data-driven’? Isn’t this still, really, about human capital, and how it’s being put to use? Uber spends a lot of money on incentivising drivers, “shippers” and food deliverers to use its platform to generate their own income, perhaps swapping what they’re already doing for this gig, or perhaps squeezing it into their spare time to make some extra cash. The amount of money Uber spends on marketing and user incentives is why they don’t yet make money on their ride-sharing business, despite the considerable fees they charge drivers, food deliverers and restaurants to use the platform. Being big, being part of more and more urban interactions taking place across every city around the world, is what matters most here. I put it to my Uber driver: Isn’t that just classic rent-seeking behaviour?
The difference here is the data, he explains to me. He says “dayta,” like an American, not “darta” like most Australians. You can’t work in tech or business these days and get away with “darta.” Uber can make all kinds of uses of the dayta created by users — which means, he explains, their brokerage service is not non-productive, in that classic rent-seeking sense. They’ve accelerated into self-driving cars, and they can also use all that dayta they’re generating to capture a granular sense of how cities really work.
Yes yes, that dayta.
It’s one of those conversations that pokes around some big topics, but won’t jump fully in. My Uber driver and I know we’re only going to be speaking for a few more fleeting moments before I jump out of the car with a cheery goodbye, trying not to slam the door too hard lest I damage my rider rating. Good luck with everything! I say.
Once out of the car, the Uber app hits me with a rating request. How was your ride today? I enthusiastically tap on the five-star option, and choose “Great conversation” to describe why my trip was so great.
We’re building the platform stack
The experience I’ve just recounted is not quite true — it’s more an amalgam of many different Uber trips I’ve taken over the past few years, and the conversations I tend to strike up with drivers. During much of Uber’s life in Australian cities, I’ve been reflecting on how platforms of this kind have been affecting the way we live in cities together.
Despite all kinds of misgivings about the kind of company Uber is — a massive, US-based outfit that fleeces the very people it seeks to “partner” with to sell its technology, and puts taxi drivers like my neighbour out of a job — I’ve become fascinated by the kinds of interactions it and similar companies have introduced.
There’s a sense of heightened sociability between strangers that seems to occur, perhaps because we’re protected by that threat of algorithmic-generated banishment if either party takes a misstep. Or maybe it’s the kind of people who have been quick to take up Uber as a transport option. As an iconic company of the “gig economy,” Uber often attracts people who aren’t looking to drive cars for the rest of their lives — which means you get to chat with people like my Uber driver, who also happened to be studying for an MBA and thinking about the future of data platforms.
Uber is also, in many senses, the realisation of a quite radical idea advocated for many years by sustainability planners. What if we could get people to stop thinking of transport through the lens of the privately held motor vehicle and instead encourage people to share their driving experience? Couldn’t this cut the number of cars on the road, and free up space for other kinds of uses?
Like the car-sharing company GoGet, founded by sustainability advocate Bruce Jeffreys, Uber advocated its way into our cities as an innovative way to get people to move around them differently. Assets once considered purely private could become shared resources. Instead of ownership being the goal, we could reduce consumption and shift towards an economy based on access.
Apart from GoGet, these companies haven’t focused on creating cities that use fewer of the planet’s scarce resources. For Uber, creating a technology platform to improve human movement was more a way to grow a company quickly — really quickly, faster than any company before, generating huge benefits for its business leaders, investors, and shareholders.
For a company like Uber, the future of cities, and how we live in them, is primarily about the possibility that digital infrastructure built today will stick around as a foundational platform for future generations, in cities all around the world, to use as their first choice. Time to go to the airport? Better Uber it. Getting people around the world to use your company name as a verb to describe some of the most basic things we do in cities is, really, the ultimate, multi-billion-dollar goal. Want to know where you’re going? Better Google it.
Those who think about cities and digital innovation are often people like my Uber driver, busy coming up with start-up business ideas in this brave new world of tech-driven urban interaction. Many, it seems, focus their minds on new ways to do takeaway food. After all, people are time poor, but they also need to eat. Why not better service the needs of those who not only lack the time or wherewithal to cook, but would also prefer not to have to actually go fetch their order?
The success of digital food delivery apps has probably caught your attention. Australia is, it seems, becoming “an Uber Eats nation,” as one journalist puts it, with online food delivery services now worth 12 per cent of all sales in the $44 billion cafe, restaurant and takeaway food industry, and one in three adults living in Australian cities reporting use of food delivery apps.
No wonder, then, that moving around our major cities now seems to involve a lot of interaction with bike-riders carrying large square boxes of food to the time-poor customers.

Title: Planetary civics: a conversation with Indy Johar
Contents:
Field note
Planetary civics: a conversation with Indy Johar
Planetary Civics Seminar, RMIT University with Indy Johar, August 2023
August 2023
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Civic Interplay
From the archive. A conversation between Indy Johar and Dr. Sarah Barns, the first in the Planetary Civics Seminar Series, supported by RMIT University.
Selected topics
Sarah Barns: As a strategic designer, what are the ways in which you could act as an intervention in that space? Would you like to speak about any projects that you are doing to tweak the value systems for something like a tree?
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Time of transformation Civic Interplay
Read along · from 16:50 in the full recording
I would argue we’re living in a one in a 400 year cycle of transformation, where our theory of seeing the world through silos and objects and individual discrete things is being challenged by seeing the world in relationship to. Like the chair that you see here, the chairs, they are a flow, right? They are a flow of materials to which they are not at this moment in time, to which they have existed before and they will exist after, not in the same form, but in other forms, either as most likely as waste somewhere.
But we see things through the theory of objects, yet actually what we don’t see and organise things through a series of flows. And I think that’s now made possible by new technology and new capabilities that technology is offering us. And so when people talk about circularity, they’re fundamentally challenging the nature of how we see the world around us.
Sarah Barns: How do we work in alliance with each other to progress these terms and these ways of thinking? Do we all need a kind of agreement around common language, to relabel, rebrand, rename things that have become almost hollow by their overuse?
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Humanism Civic Interplay
Read along · from 20:20 in the full recording
I think the real hard work is having the courage, and I think it’s courage, to re-examine ourselves. How do we respect the extraordinariness of being human? And that extraordinariness is not the deficit of the planet, because I think everything around us is pretty extraordinary. But I think there’s a sort of paradigm transformation of what it means to be human, and recognising our entanglements as a key part of being human.
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Re-examine ourselves Civic Interplay
Read along · from 21:19 in the full recording
I think one of the biggest challenges that we face is to unwind and have the courage to re-examine ourselves, and that re-examination sits at many levels, recognising that it is not, you know, my brain is not my brain, it’s a social brain. I stand on the shoulders of everyone else around me, and actually that is a material reality rather than actually some heroism of like, “Oh, aren’t I extraordinary?”
Actually recognising our entanglement at a deep level is not just an illusion, and you can go to quantum level, you know, people like David Bohm were talking about this beautifully in the 1970s. So you can go from a quantum level all the way to the social brain, you can go through microbiomes, all of this stuff, that actually there’s a fundamental re-examination of us. And I think that is the courage space right now, to be able to allow ourselves to re-examine ourselves. And I would argue that every great revolution is rooted in re-examination of what it means to be human. And I think that is the paradigm we’re in the middle of.
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Planetary species Civic Interplay
Read along · from 23:21 in the full recording
We live as a planetary relationship with each other. And we’re already living in a planetary cycle. Unfortunately, most of that planetary cycle is extractive. Most of that planetary cycle is extractive and asymmetric. But the reality is we’re already a planetary species. We’re already there.
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Coding institutions Civic Interplay
Read along · from 25:58 in the full recording
So we’ve created a world view, we’ve incorporated it, seeded it, coded it into our institutions. And the coding of our capital institutions around us creates the asymmetric extractions, externalities. A private limited company was designed to create an asymmetric landscape of effectively shielding the extraction of wealth without holding the liabilities.
So we’ve created a world view, we’ve incorporated it, seeded it, coded it into our institutions. And I think that world view that’s been coded is having to be reimagined. And that’s, I think, the paradigm leap we’re in the middle of, but it’s rooted in the courage of re-examining what it means to be human.
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Democracy and science Civic Interplay
Read along · from 26:35 in the full recording
The science behind our policy is just archaic. We just do not understand. We haven’t created the politics for this new transformation, and the politics of actually living genuinely in a quantum world, if you want to put it through that lens, living in a world of entanglement. We haven’t created the politics for it. And that’s the civilisation leap.
So I think there’s a really deep question about actually our pathways for democracy. We’ve narrowed democracy through the vote. I think that is a massive problem. And I think the vote is not sufficient to describe a 21st century democracy. And I think many people now feel entrapped in their lives, and they feel diminished in their humanity. And I think there is a corollary to that, which is that our democratic systems are no longer actually advancing a deep, meaningful democracy.
Sarah Barns: Our minds are being shaped by interrelationships with platform power, while at the same time those such as yourself are calling for a much more entangled sense of self with our more-than-human worlds. I see this bifurcation potentially happening. How do we grapple with those two almost conflicting trends in what it means to be human today?
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Technology Civic Interplay
Read along · from 28:47 in the full recording
I mean, when I talk about the entanglement, I would say machine, human, ecological entanglement. I wouldn’t put machines outside of us. And this is a really important conversation because I think one thing that we did, and I think we’ve done this in the act of othering, we’ve othered technology as much as we’ve othered trees. And when you other something, you also create a landscape of violence to that thing, and you anticipate a violence from that thing to yourself. So the distancing of things, and this was a conceptual frame, if you really go back into history, the idea of perspective, the idea of classification theory, this separation allowed for both the violence and allowed for a permission of othering. Now that distancing creates a way of seeing.
So I think in a certain thesis we created this othering and thereby a fear of technology. Whereas I think there are other cultures like Japan and other places which have not othered technology in that way. They see technology as a symbiosis and an entanglement with being human. So I think there’s something really interesting about maybe not even de-othering technology, but re-entangling ourselves with technology, and talking about a machine, human, ecological symbiosis that we’re seeing.
And this is where people like James Lovelock say this more eloquently than I will. He talked beautifully about actually, for the first time, the planet, through its sensory networks, satellites and other things, is able to become self-aware of itself. So we are able to recognise the earth is heating up. That self-consciousness at the planetary scale is the emergent, he would argue, of a planetary consciousness. And that’s an extraordinary idea, that the planet is becoming self-aware, and we are part of an intelligence system of the planet becoming self-aware. And that for the first time, the planet can not only be self-aware, it can be self-agent. So if there is a meteorite coming to hit the planet, the planet can actually do something about it, to preserve an ecological biosphere which is acting as a cooling agent to preserve life on this planet.
Sarah Barns: How do you navigate those different institutional contexts, to work within them but then also to reinvent? And, as we’re in an educational institution here, what are the ways that you see educational institutions responding to this?
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Politics of freedom Civic Interplay
Read along · from 41:18 in the full recording
I think we haven’t been able to be critical about our democratic systems because actually we’ve been locked into a 200 or 250 year paradigm, which we are going to have to reinvent, move ourselves outside industrial democracy into a new theory of agency, a new theory of freedom as well. Language like freedom has largely never been adopted by progressives because we’ve always seen it through the lens of collectivism and solidarity, but actually a freedom to care, not a freedom to escape, but a freedom to be able to be human, to thereby live in care. So how do we build a new language and taxonomy around that?
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Organisational complexity Civic Interplay
Read along · from 42:15 in the full recording
If we’re operating in complexity, which we are, there are two paradigms in complexity that are really important. And one is to operate in care. It’s a language that’s often not used because our commercial thesis is always about transactional optimisation, optimising my position versus optimising your position. Whereas to be in a relationship of care is very critical in complexity, because you do not know the second and third order implications. So you have to live through a care that requires a different attention. And the second thing is you have to operate in a relationship of learning.
So I would say that the paradigm leap for organising is that our management theory is entirely built on a theory of control, and the control from the C-suite downwards. And I think in a complex world, you have to replace the CEO with the chief learning officer. And agency needs to be at the front line, and the role of the executive is to actually scaffold the learning of the system. And coherence of a system comes through compounding learning, not through centralised control. And this is not a moral crusade from my perspective. This is just how do you deal with complexity? So if we acknowledge we’re living in a complex, entangled world, how do you build organisation to operate in complexity through a relationship of care and a relationship of compounding learning?
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
New organisations Civic Interplay
Read along · from 44:31 in the full recording
In moments like this, so one in a 400 year paradigm leap of how we relate to the world, I think we go through a moment where siloed knowledge bases have less power than polymathic knowledge bases, or entangled or intersectional knowledge bases. And that I think is a real challenge, because our universities and our learning institutions and many of our organisations are designed around siloed operations. It’s very difficult, we were talking about this earlier today, our institutional logics, our institutional incentives are all geared towards these siloed knowledge bases.
It’s been going down in pretty much all the universities. And that is because our institutional logics no longer function to actually build the polymathic disciplines, the disciplines at the intersection of disciplines. And that I think is going to be the great paradigm leap. And I think that when you compound that with machine-assisted learning, compound learning capabilities, machines which ask humans questions to direct better discovery, I think we open up a whole new paradigm of learning in that way.
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Learning institutions Civic Interplay
Read along · from 46:08 in the full recording
If you imagine the orchestration of society through a compound learning framework, I think we create whole new economies of learning, which are beyond and entangled with the institution. So it’s not that I go to the institution for four or five years of my life, but actually these are new knowledge institutions that are co-living with us in a completely different way.
So I think we’re living in a paradigm leap, which is actually in the process of going from the big macro public private divisionality to a systems entangled view, then all the way through to all the paradigms of institutions. And this manifests itself in the design, legal design of institutions, and the coding of everything around us, from employment contracts to these illusions of consultancy contracts, commodity ideas. Most of our economy is constructed through that theory of commodity or pre-prescribed value, which doesn’t work with complexity.
From the floor: I know that you can chip away in little bits, but how can you make enough change? How can we make big differences quite quickly?
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
Rate of change Civic Interplay
Read along · from 1:04:44 in the full recording
And what I’m finding interesting right now is that a year ago, a year and a half ago, a lot of what I was saying was like, I’d get invited to boardrooms, you know, and it was like, “Oh, that’s lovely, Indy. Great lunch speech. Now we can get back to business.” And what I’m finding interesting is the same CEOs and leaders are phoning me up and saying, yeah, we don’t think it works. And I had a major bank phone us up and say, yeah, we’ve been doing ESG for a while and we just don’t think it’s going to get us home. We don’t think it’s in any way commensurate to the scale of problem we’re facing.
And that recognition is starting to happen. And that to me gives me great hope, because it starts to say that what is marginal is suddenly becoming recognised as near critical. So I would say there is a much larger space of operation than I think I was imagining even a year ago. And I think all the way from monetary production, everything is going to be on the table. Literally everything is going to be on the table. The biggest challenge for democracies right now is we cannot orchestrate for the scale of transition at the speed that’s available. I was telling one major foundation recently, look, you’ve got to be allocating to reimagine democracy, right? Do not imagine the democracies that we have are going to be the democracies that are going to take us through.

Title: Transcript: a conversation with Indy Johar

Transcript: a conversation with Indy Johar
Planetary Civics Seminar, RMIT University with Indy Johar, August 2023
August 2023
Back to the recording and selected topics
Planetary Civics Seminar Series, RMIT University, 16 August 2023. Dr Sarah Barns in conversation with Indy Johar, introduced by Naomi Stead.
Transcribed by machine (Whisper) from the recording and corrected by hand for names and terms. Lightly punctuated; speech is otherwise verbatim. Timestamps refer to the full recording.
Naomi Stead [00:27]
Welcome everybody. Thank you for coming along this afternoon. My name’s Naomi Stead and I’m the director of the Design and Creative Practice Enabling Impact Platform here at RMIT. As always, or shall I say now more than ever, I’d like to begin by acknowledging the people of the Woi wurrung and Boon wurrung language groups of the Eastern Kulin Nation on whose unceded lands we conduct the business of the university. Especially now as we move towards the national referendum on the voice, I’m conscious that this is a rather difficult time for many Aboriginal people. So it’s timely to reflect on how reconciliation is a path that we walk together in fairness and openness and truth telling.
And I ask you to be an advocate for those things in the months ahead and make this referendum an occasion to draw closer together rather than be further divided. In that spirit, I pay my respects to elders past and present and all Torres Strait Islander people here today. And now it’s my great pleasure to introduce this, the first in a series of four seminars exploring the subject of planetary thinking, all of them curated and chaired by Dr. Sarah Barns and running monthly for the remainder of this year. Quite alarming to think that there’s only four and they’re monthly for the remainder of the year. The occasion for the series is the new partnership between RMIT and Dark Matter Labs, the founder and director of which Indy Johar is our special guest and Sarah’s conversation partner today.
I’ll introduce Indy and Sarah more forcibly in a moment, but first a short introduction to what this new alliance means for RMIT and perhaps for some of you here in this room. The partnership between Dark Matter Labs and RMIT is known as the Planetary Civics Initiative. It’s led on the RMIT side by Tim Marshall, who as you know is the deputy vice chancellor of the Design and Social Context College with the involvement of numerous colleagues in that college as well as the eight enabling impact platforms. The Planetary Civics Initiative has high aspirations to explore through research as well as education, as well as intervention, the great transitions that are urgently needed to move towards a more sustainable and regenerative existence on Earth.
As Sarah and Indy will shortly discuss, this requires thinking beyond current boundaries and borders, beyond the vested interests of the nation state, beyond disciplinary boundaries and so on, moving towards an entangled and intersecting mode of thinking at the scale of the planet and for the good of all living things on that planet. This planet, this collaboration will be ongoing and there will be many opportunities for you to engage and in many ways. The partnership is being formally launched at RMIT in a series of events over the week of Indy’s visit and I invite you particularly to come along to his keynote as part of the City of Melbourne’s Now or Never Festival, which will be taking place the next Monday evening at the Capitol Theatre and for which RMIT staff and students can receive discounted or free tickets.
I also warmly encourage you to get along to the exhibition Wild Hope, Conversations for Planetary Commons, which has just opened, is now open in Design Hub Gallery, Building 100 and which has an amazing series of public programs which will include a sound work by Sarah Barns. That’s enough for me. Please allow me to introduce our speakers. Indy Johar is founding director of Dark Matter Labs. An architect by training, Indy is a senior innovation associate with the Young Foundation and a visiting professor at the University of Sheffield. He co-founded Impact Hub Birmingham and Open Systems Lab and was a member of the RSA’s Inclusive Growth Commission. He’s a thought leader in system change, the future of urban infrastructure finance, outcome-based investment and the future of governance.
Sarah Barns is an RMIT Vice Chancellor’s Senior Research Fellow whose work is critically engaged with the evolution of digital urban interfaces, platforms and institutions and their implications for urban justice and connected multi-species communities. Sarah has extensive experience as a strategic advisor and consultant to government and industry and leads regenerative art strategies and projects through her creative practice Esem Projects. Take it away.
Sarah Barns [04:48]
Thank you very much, Naomi, for that introduction. It’s really good to be here today and it’s lovely to be perhaps meeting you in the audience for the first time. I would like to also acknowledge that we are, that we are gathering here today at the site of the Woi wurrung and Boon wurrung people of the Eastern Kulin Nation, people who have acted as custodians of this land and in relation to land, water, sky and many species for over 60,000 years and I think, particularly at this time, we know we have a lot to learn from these ways of being in relation to country. I myself have spent a lot of my life on Gadigal Wangal land and I also come from Wyalup (Fremantle) country.
So I would like to pay my respects to Aboriginal people from those places and to any others who are here today listening. So thanks again for joining us in this first of the seminar series attached to the Planetary Civics Initiative. As Indy Johar said, I don’t know if it was last time that you were here, Indy, but the Living Cities Forum in 2022, you remarked on the fact that we are living through a time of really intense transformation at a planetary scale and in fact, you used the analogy of living through World War II in terms of the sort of scale of transformation that we are experiencing today and only going to accelerate in coming years where the kind of the effects of global heating, but also that of the sixth mass extinction reminded that in fact, the last time a level of extinction was happening at this rate and scale was at the extinction of the dinosaurs.
That was the fifth mass extinction. So this isn’t a time that we’re really trying to grapple with in terms of its scale, but also I think, and it was another point that you raised, Indy, and many others do as well, that while these are changes that are happening at this planetary scale, they also require shifts and changes in our very relational natures, in the nature of our relational beings, how we act together as citizens, but also how we relate to materials, to matter, to country, to sky, to other species. And I think for those of us who have been around on this planet for a little while, that is quite a change.
Those of us who have been brought up in quite colonial systems, it is quite a shift in a personal transformation that is required at this time. I think that’s the kind of call to action. So the Planetary Civics Seminar Series, I thought was a good opportunity for us to invite leaders of the initiative at RMIT, and indeed, Indy from Dark Matter Labs, to really explore this kind of dialogue between the larger scale, the planetary, and also the kinds of personal transformations that we’re encountering as leaders, as strategists, as designers, as professors, as students, and so forth. So that’s really the intention of what we’re doing today.
I’m super thrilled to be in conversation with Indy Johar, a huge fan of his work. In fact, had the opportunity to share a stage with you some years ago, but don’t expect Indy to remember that. So I guess what we are doing today is really just in conversation. I’m gonna ask Indy some questions. He tells me he didn’t read them in advance, so he’s gonna be answering off the cuff, which is all the best, really, because we’re in spontaneous dialogue with each other. I like that. And then we’ll hopefully have the opportunity to open to the floor so that you too can engage in this dialogue.
So Indy, if you don’t mind, we’ll ask you, I guess I’m interested to begin with a little bit of background about you as a practitioner. Indy, you started your career as an architect, an architect of buildings, I expect, but then over the course of your career, you’ve navigated a shift towards a much larger scale of design and intervention, an architect of strategic interventions. I guess I’m interested to hear from you of how you, in fact, have navigated this transformation.
Indy Johar [09:31]
Hi, good afternoon. I suppose for me, so I think, like all things, some things come through disillusionment. I trained as an architect, and very quickly figured out architecture was a function of capital. Form follows money, as opposed to form-following function, as everyone loves to say, but actually forms follow capital, and form follows money, and what you started to realize was that actually most of architecture was working in a very particular way to optimize a theory of value, which is very limited, and secondly, what became very evident to me was actually recognizing that the building of things, because architecture is largely a function of capital and transaction, that it’s very difficult to deeply innovate in architecture.
You get service-level innovations, colors, and everything else, but actually to deeply change some of the nature of value and how you make it, it became very difficult to do, so whilst I trained as an architect, I then realized that the only way I was gonna innovate in the making of our environments was to start making things, and so we worked with people like Melissa Mean at Demos, and we worked together to build the Bristol Urban Beach. We were part of building stuff like the Impact Hub Network with Jonathan Robinson, or literally building OpenDesk, an open-source furniture company, to WikiHouse, open-source housing, and all of these things were about how do you democratize the making of place.
Democracy not as the vote, but democracy as the agency of how do you make your cities and places, and how do you build a new way of doing them in a different way. And that was my journey into making environments, and from there, it became very much about really re-examining our relationship with the world, and I can get more into that, because I think it became very evident that a lot of the logics around our environment, like a street tree, it’s a great example, a street tree is a cost to the municipality. It’s an insurance cost, and it’s a maintenance cost, yet all the ecological benefits are yet unpriced.
So for example, the cooling effect of trees, or the flood risk management of trees, or effectively the health benefits of trees. And so also trees are largely 96% males, male trees as opposed to male and female, because they’re easier to manage in terms of actually the waste production. So what we end up with is high levels of asthma rates as a result of that. So what we’ve optimized as capital in the kind of allocation of our environment, and that’s why after 10 years, most cities will chop down their trees and replace them, because that’s the management cost becomes much higher. So what I started to realize was the built environment was structured and coded by our accounting logics and the way we saw value and what was not being valued.
And that was a kind of a bit of an epiphany for me in terms of actually transforming sort of our thoughts around the world and how do you make it and what were the underlying issues. And that’s where Dark Matter Labs came from.
Sarah Barns [12:59]
Thank you. In terms of that question about the ways in which the built environment and the built environment professions value certain services over others, in the response to that as a sort of strategic designer and leading a strategic design agency, what are the kind of ways in which you could act as an intervention in that space? Would you like to speak about any projects that you are doing to actually kind of tweak the value systems for something like a tree, for example?
Indy Johar [13:37]
Yeah, I mean, so there’s several structural things that I would say are really important, then we can get to the projects. First thing is I think it’s very difficult to consult innovation. So if you have a consultancy contract, you’re bound to the idea of what is the terms of reference of that contract. So most of the work we do is in partnership with and we will raise our own money to do the innovations around the things that we think about. So what’s the nature of the relationship that you set up, I think is really important. Second is the nature of the organization. I mean, two things about this that are really important.
So, you know, Dark Matter Labs, one of the things that I recognize is I went from originally starting in a small architecture practice, which was seven people, and it went up to 70 people. When we were seven people, we were designing handrails with nodules in because of tactile memories, one of the last memories to go for care homes. When we were 70 people, we were designing colorful facades because the only thing you can control as a principle of a practice when you get to 70, 100 people is basically the facades. So you get reduced. So what ends up happening is that the organization, the theory of management and control transforms what you design and how you design.
So that was the other thing for me is that how do you build an organization which isn’t based around the theory of sense sort of hero leadership and hero control of design? And what does that mean to build a different type of organization which is not based on control, but it’s based on learning. So two paradigms. One, actually the nature of the contract. Two, the nature of the organization. And the third one is the nature of the disciplines. So in our practice, we’ve got finance people, lawyers, accountants, artists, anthropologists, designers. It is substantially actually multi-transdisciplinary. And when we talk about transdisciplinary in the built environment field, it means you’ve got an engineer on board and maybe you’ve got sort of environmental engineer or a landscape designer.
And that just isn’t enough. So how do you build deeply transdisciplinary teams actually at core level? So I think that’s just the root level issues. And that then allows you to be able to then fundamentally look at the world through a different lens. So we’re doing a project, let’s use all the way from series of projects when one is re-imagining the idea of a house, a house which owns itself. So you don’t own it, nobody else owns it.
