But it’s also very clear to say that actually, if we were to get into a theory of violence, which is one of the scenarios that we’re really living with against seven billion people, and I’m using that sample as a metaphor in that way, it is almost certain that we as a species, if we unleash the violence against seven billion people, the level of planetary trauma we will set up will almost certainly mean that we will not survive because nuclear weapons, bioweapons, various other things will be unleashed, which will almost self-terminate us.
So the paradigm leap that we’re sitting in is that we are either sitting in a world of mutually assured destruction, use a phrase from the 1960s and ’70s, or we’re living in a world of mutually assured thriving, and it is a fork. And I think, so in that fork between mutually assured destruction and mutually assured thriving, mutually assured thriving requires us to deeply reinvent the epistemology and the kind of fundamentals of this world. So what I’m also seeing is capital, not all of it, but the primaries of capital, i.e. the people that actually own the wealth, not the wealth managers, ‘cause they’re just functioning, they’re algorithms.
Most wealth managers are just algorithm, algorithmic allocators of capital. They, like I said, they will chop down the trees because that’s what the accounting says. That’s the most efficient way of doing it. They are functionally just extensions of mathematics and accounting, but the primaries of capital are starting to understand the self-terminating nature of the risks that we’re facing. So yes, it’s dark. At the same time, I also think that there is a new form of recognition emerging at that level. The next part is the politics of this. So there’s a capital power, but then there’s often what I would say is the everyday politics, and there’s two things to that.
One, that I often, so I have given talks in everyday public realms like Sheffield and Birmingham on a neighborhood level, and I still give these sort of talks. And I’m often accused, if I’m really honest, people will come to me and say, “Oh, Indy, your ideas are just free-floating out here,” everyday reality. And what was really interesting, I had a sort of 89-year-old man walk up to me. It was like this was Birmingham, Link Road, neighborhood festival. He walked up to me and said, “Indy, I didn’t get everything you said. However, you put words into what I was feeling. I think we should not underestimate how deeply people are feeling and experiencing this reality, yet they do not have the language and the frames to unlock it, and we often try to communicate, but we don’t try to have conversations.
And I think the politics of transitions will be based out of conversation, not communication. And I think this requires us to actually frame, this is why the language has to be reimagined. Like I talk about a new theory of freedom, because I see people’s realities of being entrapped, but a freedom not to violence to escape the system, but the freedom to actually be in care with the world around us. So I have an everyday hope, because I can see there’s a pathway to the everyday politic, which isn’t as divisional as everyone wants to make out, because I think that’s based on a form of opinion formation.
And I’ll give you a, again, just a final example. We did a piece of work where we got a random bunch of people together, literally, off the street, and asked them, “How many people like universal basic income?” This was five years ago. And 78% of people randomly in the room off the street said, “We don’t like universal basic income, because everyone’s gonna be lazy, they’re gonna sit in their rooms, drink beer, and that’s it.” 78%. They spent the day together, and they were in discussion, we had lectures and talks and everything else. And that whole example it’s flipped from 78% against to 82% pro. I thought it was because, you know, all these talks, but when you did the analysis of the survey, they said it wasn’t that.
What it was was that actually they thought the guy with the beard and the funny hat, was no different from them. So when they were in the room together, we de-othered the people around them. And once you de-othered the room, they made different choices and different frameworks of seeing the world. And suddenly the othering was what was creating the violence of distrust. But as soon as you de-othered the room, the policy landscape transformed itself. The place landscape of what was possible transformed itself. So I acknowledge the violence in the system, but I also acknowledge the deep signals that are emerging and the necessity. I don’t think we actually have a choice.
We can sit there and argue the choices in mutually assured destruction or mutually assured thriving. It’s a fork, not a choice. And life, to quote Jurassic Park, life wants to live. And I think this is the choice that we have. And this is why this paradigm leap is a necessity, not a choice. And it is a duty for us, not a choice, not a political choice, to build and unfold this reality.
Sarah Barns [01:00:03]
Thank you. It’s one of the things that I guess, I admire about what you are doing is that you are re-imagining and rethinking, but also providing kind of prototypes and examples and interventions that I think we can all learn from. So I see that as being a hugely positive intervention for all of us and a way to kind of act during this time of change. I guess we probably have time for one more quick question, but then we’ll have to wrap up this conversation. And we do have some drinks and nibbles in the foyer. But just I am conscious that we wanted to have enough time for conversation.
So just time for one more question if there is one. Otherwise we can adjourn and have conversations outside. I’m not seeing any hands or we’ve got one hand in the corner. Is that, that’s okay.
Audience member [01:01:05]
Firstly, thank you, Indy. That was extraordinary. And I think each of us are going to walk out of this room thinking even a little bit differently because I guess you get a lot of people that you get to speak to who are already going to that right side of the fork. So my question really is about that. How can you make changes? Because I know that you can chip away in little bits, but how can you make enough change? And is that hope or is it confidence that you can get enough people from the planetary global population to be heading that way in time for us to be making it down that path before it’s too late?
So it’s not a question of, it’s not me being negative because I absolutely love everything you say. I’m just really thinking, how can we make big differences quite quickly?
Indy Johar [01:02:29]
It’s a great question. And I think I, I think it requires more of us to work on this problem. That’s the first thing I would say. I think many more of us need to be deeply engaging the challenges that we face. And I still see, let’s be honest, I need RMIT to be transforming itself radically, right?
Audience member [01:03:04]
[Partly inaudible] Yeah, I’m not talking about innovation and learning a language is strange. Our notions of change are so easy.
Indy Johar [01:03:12]
Absolutely. So I think the question is, how do we all start to act? If you’re a CEO, challenge your theory of organizing, challenge your theory of orchestration. Challenge yourself to become the chief learning officer, not the control officer. How do you build a different, and that requires you to change pay scales, by the way. It requires you to whole transform contract theory. It drives you to transform all sorts of risk models in the organization. It tries to do all sorts of things. So I think it requires all of us to be part of it. Second part is I think this will require many, many layers of intervention all the way from central banks, horizon one.
Central banks will actually break up single interest rate models to differential interest rate models. So if you’re allocating for nature, you might have a negative interest rate, where if you’re buying consumables and waste driven systems, you might have a 10, 15% interest rate. So we will need all sorts of macro things. We’ll also need to reimagine our theory of what’s the mental health of a city? Is that an asset? So how do you reimagine? Currently mental health is an individual issue. Why? Why is it not a population value? How do you think about collective intelligence of a city? So reimagining our asset classes of the 21st century.
Reimagining soil as an asset class, not just the trees, ‘cause soil is actually a fundamental asset of society. Reimagining the theory of agency. I think these are gonna have to be deeply coded in. And what I’m finding interesting right now is that a year ago, a year and a half, year ago, a lot of what I was saying was like, I’d get invited to boardrooms, you know? And it was like, oh, that’s lovely, Indy. Great lunch speech, now we can get back to business. And what I’m finding interesting is those same CEOs and leaders are phoning me up and saying, yeah, we don’t think it works.
And I had a major bank phone us up and said, yeah, we’ve been doing ESG for a while, and we just don’t think it’s gonna get us home. We don’t think it’s any way commensurate to the scale of problem we’re facing. And that recognition is starting to happen. And that to me gives me great hope because it starts to say that what is marginal is suddenly becoming recognized as near critical. So I would say there is much larger space of operation than I think I was imagining even a year ago. And I think all the way from monetary production, everything is going to be on the table.
Literally everything is going to be on the table. The biggest challenge for democracies right now is we cannot orchestrate for the scale of transition at the speed that’s available. And I think that I think is a real issue. So if I was, I was telling one major foundation recently to say, look, you’ve got to be allocating to reimagine democracy, right? Do not imagine the democracies that we have are going to be the democracies that are gonna take us through. So I would invite us all to start to build those new types of institutions and capabilities. And I think that’s just going to exist everywhere around us.
And the institutions that start to make this transition now will start to see the value. I think we’re no longer marginal. That’s one thing I’d say. At Dark Matter, we’re working all the way from banks all the way through to public institutions. So I think the conversation has shifted in under a year and this thing will scale. I think the world is changing very rapidly. Not through any moral issue, by the way. It’s changing because actually this is the only way of organizing. Complexity demands a new theory of organizing. That demand is now fundamental and clear. And that requires a new type of institutional model. That requires actually a new way of relating and organizing.
So that’s where I sit with great hope and it’s deeply rooted. And I go back to my old point. Actually, it’s deeply rooted in this thesis of life, wants to live. Actually, we’re going to have to find a way. And it’s going to be a much more structural transformation. It goes back to the earlier conversation. More commensurate with a World War II rebuild of Europe and other places. That is the scale of transformation we’re seeing. And ideologically, it’s more like a 400 year transformation. Newtonian enlightenment. It’s actually equivalent to how Newtonian enlightenment constructed a world view. And we’re going to recast that into a quantum world view, which I think is the big arc in history that we’ll see ourselves through.
So I sit with great hope. Because I think that’s an extraordinary invitation for a generation of us. The final point I’ll make. Unfortunately, this is not going to be your kids. It’s all of you. Because it’s going to happen much faster than everyone’s talking about. There is no handover to, yes, we’re going to hand over to the next generation. They’re going to be the ones that do it. It’s all of us now. We don’t have a choice. That’s where it is. Thank you.
Sarah Barns [01:08:02]
Thank you very much, Indy. I’d like to thank you. It’s been incredible to have you here speaking with RMIT staff and students today. I think we all feel really, really appreciative of your time. I personally find what you have to say incredibly inspiring to my work. And I hope you all have as well been inspired today. And thought provoked, as we say. Now, important to mention that Indy is giving a keynote presentation as part of the Now or Never Festival and as part of the Wild Hope Initiative. That is on Monday night at the Capitol Theatre. There are discount codes. If you haven’t yet booked your ticket.
And I believe the discount code is quite easy to remember. It’s RMIT student or RMIT staff. So if you remember those things, and if you would like to hear Indy at his keynote speech, I will certainly be there on Monday night. So please do come along and book. Thanks again, Indy.

Planetary Civics Seminar Series, RMIT University, 29 February 2024. Dr Sarah Barns in conversation with Rosi Braidotti and Fiona Hillary.
Transcribed by machine (Whisper) from the recording and corrected by hand for names and terms. Lightly punctuated; speech is otherwise verbatim. Timestamps refer to the edited recording.
Sarah Barns [00:00]
Hello everyone, microphones on, microphones on. My name is Sarah. For those of you who haven’t met me before, as Tim said, I recently joined RMIT as a Senior Vice Chancellor’s Research Fellow at the Centre for Urban Research. It is with great pleasure that I welcome Rosi and Fiona into this first Planetary Civics Seminar for the year. Before I go further, I did want to also acknowledge that we are having this conversation on the unceded lands of the Woi wurrung and Boon wurrung people of the Eastern Kulin Nation. And I’d also like to acknowledge the wisdom of the elders and their custodianship of country, of sea country, of sky country, and the ways in which that I think has a critical role to play in our ideas about posthumanism and planetary thinking.
What a wonderful way to start the series this year and we are here to bring in dialogue, I suppose, the ideas of Rosi Braidotti, Fiona Hillary, and I guess the stage that has been set around the concepts of planetary civics. We have big ideas to discuss. We are talking about coalescing forms of crises, as well as the need for transformation in the ways in which we are relating to each other, to materialities, to institutions like the university, but also to other species, to nature as a whole, to symbols, to mythologies. So it’s a wonderful context to do this conversation with Rosi. We have big things to discuss, but I suppose in line with ideas of Rosi’s around the need for embodied situated practices, I did want to begin our conversation today as we do with the seminar series to actually kind of situate ourselves in a time and space, time and place even, even better.
We are, you know, I have here two scholar, practitioners, activists at different stages of their careers. And so I wanted to open this conversation, I guess, with a question to both of you. Rosi, I will begin with you. You have recently retired from a formal position at Utrecht, and now happily we can announce an affiliation with RMIT. But you are acting in a more, shall we say, nomadic relationship to institutions. And I’d like you to share a little bit about how that is influencing your agenda around the post humanities.
Rosi Braidotti [02:29]
Thank you so much. Does this thing work? Probably not. You can hear me. So I’m very emotional. It’s my first coming out as honorary professor. I mean, what do I, [laughter] I hope that you will not be disappointed. [applause] Thank you, thank you, thank you. Amazing. So it’s not as if I left Utrecht on my own free will. In Europe, they kick you out. Have you reached a certain age? I thought, oh, really already? But I must say that I am very honored, but also very fortunate in being able to open a new phase where I hope to through design and media to actually apply some of the theories that I’ve developed over decades of very happy work in an old European research university.
I have nothing but love and respect for Utrecht, but applied it is not. It’s speculative and wonderful. So to have that possibility, RMIT is ideal. I’m a Melburnian. I have family here. And Stelarc and I go way back and Cookie. And I wanted to remind you that Cookie was created by the Braidottis, just in case you didn’t know. And now there’s another Braidotti venue that still is going and that is Revolver. So the Braidottis have done a lot for this town. Long live my brother who has done that. So what I am interested in is applying in a specific empirical way as a materialist and critical posthumanist the space of the city as a unit of reference to try to figure out how we deal with what I call the convergence of crisis which I prefer to define as challenges.
On the one hand, the huge momentous technological push. On the other hand, the clear obvious environmental devastation and the growth of social inequalities, social injustices. Not to mention the warfare which has become the new necropolitical regime of our times. So city urban spaces as the ideal testing ground for some of the things that we’re trying to do. And to do that, you need a transdisciplinary framework. And that is one of the strengths of both the planetary civics project and the posthuman labs that I’ve been developing with Fiona Hillary over the years. And the materialism school that I’ve been developing with Anna Hickey-Moody over the years as well.
This is a bastion of materialist thinking. So this cooperation goes way back. And here is, I find myself incredibly fortunate to be able to actually apply some of this and getting a reality check. So I’m immensely proud and immensely grateful for this opportunity. But I delegate some to you, Fiona, different moment. Although you wish you were retired sometime.
Sarah Barns [05:19]
Fiona, yes, I’d love to hear from you. Your relationship with Rosi, how is it shaping your practice currently? And I suppose over the last few years of engagement, what has been the impact of your relationship with her in terms of your practice today?
Fiona Hillary [05:37]
Thanks, Sarah. Working with Rosi began probably in 2017, I think we first met in a chance encounter when she was here launching the Posthuman Glossary. And from that moment, I guess we started working together, thinking about the role of art in philosophy and, I guess, the applied practices that we use, the material practices we use. And Rosi invited me to join the Utrecht Summer School. And I curated, along with a range of artists across time, artists’ laboratories. So it was where we stepped out of the lecture theater and into different ways of creative thinking with the participants of the Utrecht Summer School. And that’s given rise to the work with Troy Innocent and the Australian Posthuman Summer Lab that we’ve just returned from.
There might be a few weary faces in the audience here today after returning from the beech forest in the Otways. So exploring how different practitioners engage with thinking with more than human species, non-human species, technology, and how we generate ways of being together. So Rosi has been pivotal to my thinking in terms of how we understand our situated practices in the world, how we come to navigate our relational being in contact with human and non-human and the more than human.
Rosi Braidotti [07:15]
If I could quickly annotate it, it works the other way around as well. It liberates me to be caught in an intergenerational chain of transmission in so many ways. First of all, I don’t have to teach the Posthuman Summer School in Utrecht anymore because after 11 years of coming on my nose, I will teach something but totally unrelatedly. I will teach myself for a few years now. It’s called A Week with Rosi. And it’s a small boutique, totally different story. And it allows me to then open a chapter, which is how to age radically and gracefully within institutions. And I’m going to work very hard on age as a political project and embracing aging, weaponizing it as a mode of radicalization as opposed to denying it and hotter than your daughter type of television program.
Because baby boomers are now the answer. So I want to become a good ancestor. And in a sense, this intergenerational linkage allows me to do that. So again, I’m very fortunate. But also liberated it. I actually don’t have to carry the Posthuman.
Sarah Barns [08:22]
A radical ancestor perhaps, Rosi?
Rosi Braidotti [08:25]
A radical ancestor? I hope so. I think old age has to be a moment of re-radicalization. And if I can, if I’m healthy enough for the institutions, it’s always a fight. Rest reassured, I should not be throwing bombs around. However, I will have the critical edge and the critique of power that comes from thinking that in some ways, you have nothing left. Nothing more to lose and a lot more to offer. And I also, by being radical, can protect the younger ones who have to deal with institutional pressures. You can’t really rock the boat. Donna Haraway has taught me this. And she’s 10 years older than me.
And she says, we have to radicalize so that the young can put up with this neoliberal nonsense. And I think that’s a very good formula.
Sarah Barns [09:07]
I dearly hope you can help us all. And they do say that women become more radical as we age. And I believe that to be the case myself. Thank you.
Rosi Braidotti [09:18]
Long way to go, you’re young.
Sarah Barns [09:21]
I’ve got more radicalizing to do. Listen, I wanted to turn to some of the critical themes around this platform here that we have of the planetary civics, which is, I suppose, underpinned by really this notion of crisis. And in rereading some of your work in the last few weeks, you talk about, and I think referencing Spivak, that the condition of crisis is something that is really endemic or the modus operandi of the humanities. And also, we might say, of modernism itself. It’s certainly nothing new. But I love, and maybe this connects to your point about continuing to radicalize, but I love your point about the affirmative and the place of the affirmative ethic in response to crisis.
I’d like to just ask you to reflect on this ethic that you do bring to the idea of crisis and what we can learn from you in the planetary civics program.
Rosi Braidotti [10:18]
And I have four minutes, right? Great. So it is Socrates, not Spivak, that says that the crisis is the modus operandi of philosophy. And it is intrinsically generative. And it’s not a term that I use a lot of the polycrisis with regard to Morin, and it’s now very fashionable. I like to talk about convergences of problematic areas— technology, environmental depletion, social injustices, and more and more nuclear warfare. According to the think tanks, we are six seconds from midnight. It is the worst that we have ever been since the Cold War, what is happening in terms of our security and the wars that we’re in. And so it’s like the Cold War heating up again, which, for an ancestor— and all the person is quite extraordinary.
So I want to keep things very grounded. I am a materialist philosopher trained in the French Australian tradition with Foucault and Deleuze, which means a critique of dialectical materialism, of historical materialism, and also a critique of the hysterical materialism of psychoanalysis, trying to reground the discussion in the critical neo-Spinozist philosophies that we know through Deleuze and the French things. So terrible that the French thing is the French thing. That the magnificent European philosophies are meta, that allow us to think the continuum between body and mind, nature, culture, without having to go to hippie Californian philosophies for it. You can really do it with Spinoza. You can do it with Leibniz.
You can do it with Nietzsche. You can do it with a lot of the materialists. You can do it with the Sydney School and the Melbourne School of Materialism that, in my book, I always pay tribute to, from Val Plumwood to Genevieve Lloyd’s great Spinoza to Moira Gatens and Elizabeth Grosz to the Melbourne School that all of us belong to. So trying to emphasize the generative potential of the situation that we’re in. I don’t use the term planetary. I do use interconnections. I don’t use entanglements either, because I don’t know what it means, but I have my terminology, which is the assemblages. Again, the bit of jargon I sense that we are made of things and relationship that we meet as we go.
And I think accounting for them requires cartographies. So I am a map maker. I’ve learned a lot from indigenous map making. You do cognitive mapping. You draw the steps of a certain process of knowledge, and knowledge comes with a relationship of power. You do know that. If you don’t have your grant, you can’t do research. That’s knowledge as power. It’s right there. You don’t have to go very far. But also the amount of capital we’re investing in certain type of technologies rather than others, why the environmental humanities have a tenth of the budgets of the digital humanities or of the medical humanities, which are massive sectors of the economy, talking about the humanities.
So I’ve become concerned with what kind of mappings do we do together. All mappings are relational. We need to exchange and comment. So the cartographies and the imagination and the creativity that goes with them remains the methodology. In this— and I’m almost over my 40 minutes— the role of the humanities, or rather the struggle of the humanities as areas of knowledge in dealing with the displacement of the human that happens in the post-human convergence. And for me, the post-human convergence is really— it’s already here. It’s something that is happening under our noses. It is the end of a certain type of humanism that assumed universalistic rights for everybody.
Feminism, post-colonial, decolonial, indigenous theories had been critiqued in that for decades. But now the impossibility of universal values is clear to everybody. And the specter of relativism is making the Steve Bannons of this world a return to fascist philosophy of unity and strength and truth. And one god, one country, one, one, one. Out of fear for this relative relativism that comes with the end of post-humanism. So the post-human has post-humanism in it, but it also has post-anthropocentrism in it. It’s displacement of species, hierarchy. And that’s much more difficult if you’re doing humanities or social sciences. I don’t think sociology is doing any better than literature. On the contrary, I would argue that it’s the other way around in terms of coping with the organization of knowledge in today’s institutions.
And the shutdowns of humanities faculties. And University of Kent just two weeks ago, humanities shutdown. Denmark has shut down, I think, three, four. It’s such shutdowns. They’re simply deleting the humanities faculties. So here we go. Who cares? I went into the university to bring feminism, critical theory, the long march through the institutions. We critique the power of men, a man of reason, think Genevieve Lloyd. And yet, I would never have expected them to become extinct, to be canceled because only data matters, only STEM matters. What is this? So there is a strange moment where critical theory needs to be very creative to cope with the perverse, unexpected results of a convergence of crisis that we brought upon ourselves.
And one of my missions is to make sure that the propositional affirmative charge of critical theories, feminism, race, that all of that is ferried across the great big divide that is now happening between the old and the new constructions of knowledge. And make sure that the post humanities have the critical edge and they’re not just a veneer for a neoliberal takeover of what’s left of the university. It wasn’t quite four minutes, was it?
Sarah Barns [16:11]
Thank you, thank you. No, I was at an industry event last week, which was discussing that big topic of AI. And there was someone in the audience who piped up and said it’s really shocking. AI is not only affecting all of our cities and our infrastructures. Now we’re getting to this point where AI is actually affecting our minds and our attention and our consciousness. And as though this was a kind of a new frontier in a way. And I think I certainly have found your ideas about the kind of constitution of the self as being not kind of, it’s not an instrumental relationship that technology has on us.
We are always being constituted by the material relations that are intrinsically data-fied, if you like, and generative. So those kind of collapsing, oh, we’ve got an interesting slide now. The collapsing distinctions between the physical and the digital, your work I think really penetrates through those debates to say it’s too simplistic to say technology is impacting us. We are already created through these generative processes. Something that, I mean, I’d love you to reflect on this, but to me, I was really interested in your idea of kind of process ontology as a way to respond to these ideas. And I think your kind of situated and embodied practice feels like it’s very much a resistant to the sort of dehumanizing effects of technology.
Would you like to comment on this space, I suppose?
Rosi Braidotti [17:49]
I will delegate AI to Fiona, who has concrete examples. For me, AI is just a very sophisticated forms of computational statistics. They know everything, but they only know that. And after which the serious thinking begins. But I know it’s simplified. I love technologies, but a couple of other things I would like to say, however. I think our culture, Western culture has chosen a form of posthumanism which has become so dominant that we don’t even see it and we don’t call it by its name. And that is transhumanism. Technology will save us. And if technology creates problems, more technology will solve the problems created by technology. Whether it is climate change, or whether it is dyslexia, whether it is the fact that our kids can’t read three lines, otherwise they have a nervous breakdown.
Whether it is suppression of jobs coming with the new forms of automation. The entire port of Rotterdam, I think, runs on 2,000 people. The rest is automated. More technology will save us. Geo-engineering, CO2 capture, more of that. That is completely in place. And I think this is where critical posthumanism is very different from other forms, including what Indy has been saying. Transhumanism is already here. It’s working, it’s all around it. It’s the dominant way, but we don’t call it that. We call it human-centered technology, AI-aided. Yeah, the machine support, like, really. So from that moment on, my critique begins. First of all, how did transhumanism come to be hegemonic without anybody actually being asked about it?
We have had critical transhumanism, like Stelarc, experimenting with technologies for decades. In a democratic, open way, saying, what can we do with it? What can a body do? How much can a body take? Did anybody ever question, ask us which direction? We wanted to go with this. Did Elon Musk ever ask our permission to colonize the moon, to jump on Mars, to get the minerals, to fund the lithium battery, given the cobalt is so difficult to mine and China owns most of it? Question mark. And did anybody ask our permission, when Elon Musk lent a rocket to send off Jeff Koons’s art to the moon as the first work of art of humanity to go in outer space?
Did anybody consult us on this? Happened last week. Did you even notice this? Is transhumanism in place, or is transhumanism in place? That’s a crucial point, because so far as we think, oh, posthumanism is something to come, it’s a very different type of discussion. Sorry, it’s right here. But we are calling it other things. So this is what we need. The cartography is so powerful. Let’s terminologies, clear definitions, boundaries, borders. And then I love technology. I would love to be enhanced. I have no problems with that. But can I decide if I want an ear in my arm, which is that, like I said, for decades, or whether I want to be prosthetically enhanced?
Can we have a social democratic approach to this? Or is it to be top down in what Fukuyama calls the soft eugenics? Do you love that? The soft eugenics of the posthuman condition. That’s pretty terrifying. If […] is to happen, I want to play a role in it. I want to have some discussion of it and not it to be decided for me. So I think cartography is a power absolutely crucial here. And the embodied, embedded, relational, affective presence of real people. Subjectivity. Subjectivity and becoming subject is always the theme that is missing from the conversation. And it’s not in actor-network theory. It certainly is not in transhumanism.
It’s not in most STEM, sadly, in any sociology today. STS, science and technology studies, all aligned with Bruno Latour so that we don’t have to ask the question of who is the subject here? Who are the embodied subjects that actually carry the project, are involved in the project? Is anybody in the room? Or are there only systems and networks? So this old-fashioned emphasis on subjectivity. And it breaks my heart that it should become old-fashioned. And so completely obsolete is already the notion of human agency to say, but we’re all becoming technology-aided subject, but we are subject. So working on the notion of subjectivity, remembering the missing people, the marginal people, remembering those who are not part of the equation.
So bearing testimony for the missing ones. As I said in my valedictory speech, which I recommend that you listen to, because it’s a great piece of rhetoric. It’s a great piece. It’s from the heart. Missing people and bearing witness of the ones that are missing. This is where we differ for transhumanism, which is a highly eugenic, highly selective, capital intensive, top-down, completely in-place system, which is also contributing to the erosion of the humanities and of the soft social sciences as old-fashioned topics and areas of study that nobody wants. And when, in fact, those narratives, those rhetorical skills, that understanding the depths of language and all, is crucial more than ever.
You don’t switch Rosi off on subjectivity.
Sarah Barns [23:12]
Thank you, Rosi. Thank you. And I think it’s the Posthuman Summer Lab. Fiona, your work as a public artist, you are doing the work or kind of bringing these ideas into public spaces and into kind of novel forums, like going to the Otways to explore what is the quarry in all of its many manifestations. I guess I’m interested to hear from you on what is the practice of working in an institution like the university in a world that might treat these kind of practice seriously. What could it be?
Fiona Hillary [23:52]
I think the role of a project like the Australian Posthuman Summer Lab is to be always connected and connected to the world through industry, through participants, through radical thinking, through new ways of experiencing the world. So the quarry, for those of you that don’t know, from these are the projects we do together, […] and […], and they became an industry partner in the Australian Posthuman Summer Lab. And with Troy Innocent and Chris Speed came out with us also to explore, I guess, the wildness of cities. Chris’s point was that we never leave cities. We are always of the city we are located with. And the quarry was providing the city with roadways and railways and a whole raft of— which is now an obsolete quarry.
And Joe and Millie’s task is to regenerate the quarry. And part of their project is to look at different ways of regeneration as opposed to filling it with water or filling it with rubbish and closing the gate. A lot of the conversations that Troy and myself and the other lab facilitators were having and the participants was how do we contribute to this notion of regeneration and what does it mean? So it’s meaning making. We’re on the edge of meaning making through our creative practices. And our questions, so many questions arose. I’m not sure how many answers arose. One of the beautiful things that came about through collaborating with Rosi and Narweet Carolyn Briggs, with Troy’s support was a mapping across posthumanism and Boon Wurrung knowledges and how they relate to each other.
And that gave us a framework to think with for the week, which I think was a really dynamic, interesting, and a much needed conversation. One of our colleagues, Emily Jones, speaks about the rights of nature. And I think at the crux of all of those kind of ways of thinking is how we work with indigenous knowledges. So it was a really pivotal part of the lab and I think a really generative way of framing some possibilities. Thank you.
Sarah Barns [26:22]
And I guess the work of regenerative futures and regenerative practices is also a really central kind of project of design and social context at the moment, obviously, with the appointment of Chris Speed. Very, very happy to have you here as new professor of practice in regenerative futures. I hope I got that right. And I think the term regeneration is an interesting one because it does actually throw in the mix all kinds of different practices that include more traditional practices of sustainability and ecological regeneration. But there is also this recognition of the more than human and the need to think outside of traditional humanistic or human-centred approaches to think in terms of multi-species beneficiaries, but also First Nations knowledge systems, the ideas of deep time that we are working across quite conceptual kind of new beginnings and ancient ways of connecting with country.
And all of these are in the mix, I think, when we think about regeneration. And it brings me, I guess, to my next question for you, Rosi, which is to reflect a little bit on the ways in which, I guess, right now, we are a renaissance of recognition around First Nations thinking and Indigenous thinking for the way we understand processes of time and of history and connection to the more than human. In your career, you’ve seen such a shift in your earlier days, perhaps here in Australia, in our relationship to Indigenous knowledge systems. So I was interested to hear you reflect on, I guess, how you felt that shift take place in your own intellectual formation.
Rosi Braidotti [28:13]
Good one. And again, four minutes.
Sarah Barns [28:15]
I didn’t say it’s four minutes. We’ve got a little bit more than that.
Rosi Braidotti [28:18]
So the conceptual framework is pretty steady from the early days to today. And it is the idea that we humans is not an entity, is not unitary, that being human is differential, that we’re not human in the same way to the same degree, that the differences, the structure of becoming human, are really gigantic in terms of ethnicity, a class, race, sexuality, gender, all of that. And from the beginning, my knowledge claims have been situated on the side of the excluded of the marginal, of those that are different from— different from what? From the dominant idea of the human. As a student of Genevieve Lloyd, the man of reason was the course that I got as an introduction to the history of philosophy at the ANU in the 1970s.
How lucky was I? I got it as my undergraduate education. So there is an idea of a man of reason that is the standard, the gold standard of human knowledge, is the one that the astronauts of NASA have as a patch on their suits. So it’s already on the moon as well. These people and the moon, what is it? So there is that understanding of knowledge from the margin, the wisdom and the knowledge of the margin. I think that’s crucial. It positions a generation and a tradition of materialist thinking that is not reduced.
[The recording ends here.]

Title: Mystical language loops: A moment with Walter Benjamin
Contents:
Essay
Mystical language loops: A moment with Walter Benjamin
A refreshed newsletter focus for 2025, and an actual-imaginary encounter with Walter Benjamin to guide a mystical love of language & storytelling.
October 2024
Picture this. You’re walking down the footpath, phone in hand, scrolling the morning emails. It’s the morning ‘house cleaning’ routine, clearing out the junk and spam accrued from the night before. Delete Delete Delete.
You’re walking down the street in a town called Melbourne, Australia. The bluestone tiles you walk upon are cracked and uneven. You are looking at your phone as your feet negotiate the uneven surface. Because, well, you know you can.
Today, you’re deleting without mercy. You want to feel in control of your life. You want to feel like you’re one of those zero-inbox people who walk this earth. It won’t change the immovable, immense substrata that is your unread email collection, but it still feels good.
Then you hear a voice, it’s his voice, speaking to you just now.
“Every morning brings us the news of the globe, and yet we are poor in noteworthy stories.”*
Gasp! It’s Walter Benjamin. The one you could never let go of.
A German philosopher and cultural critic born in the closing decade of the nineteenth century, Benjamin is the thinker you may speak to all your days.
Benjamin, who used his love and adoration of language to express, in both wonderment and dismay, the disorientations of the emergent machine age: the cacophany of voices on the radio, the clanging of the mechanical street cars, the bewilderments of the exotic shopping arcades popping up around his beloved Paris.
Benjamin, who saw through the tactics of journalistic jargon, its smoothing of the lively world. Which he saw as training minds everywhere to accept this version of events, the world painted by the mass-produced newspaper article.
Benjamin, who brought such care and devotion to the happenings of the world, and to what he saw as the radical remaking of the western mind. Who used the arts of memory to disrupt the steady-smooth passages of modernisation. Who was, perhaps, the first remix artist, who saw that strange insertions of the past could be a way to undermine the tyranny of the now, towards something more radical, more emergent, more unstable.
Dear Benjamin, he’s always watching the world, even now. Walter Benjamin image sourced from Esther Leslie’s essay marking the 75th anniversary of Benjamin’s death, published by Verso.
Here’s here with you, at this moment, in this strange infosphere modulating and shaping your days. This line of his, it will never let you go.
You turn his words around in your mind. What did he mean by that, really? When we have news of the globe surrounding us, how can we be poor in noteworthy stories? Why is he telling me this, now?
The coming of the ‘new media’ age brought with it new social tensions. Benjamin responded with a book ‘The Storyteller’. Source: Times Wide World Photos.
Benjamin language training
You’ve trained yourself on this way of thinking for some time now. To let Benjamin’s disposition be your disposition. You’ve been taught to interpret the world as Benjamin would have done - which means to dispute, but not to suppress. Instead, to endow the everyday with something slightly magical and mystical.
Benjamin saw ‘noteworthy stories’ as the stories that shape the realities of our lives. ‘News of the globe’ is the information that spreads easily, but may not be what we need or value. News of the globe is the infosphere. As Benjamin saw it, people would increasingly need to negotiate between information and stories, between shared experience and its denial. They would need to discern the difference between the two.
Why did Benjamin call out to you just now, then?
You suspect Benjamin was asking you to pay more attention to how information is shaping you. Asking you to claim the right to craft your own particular version of events, your own story, not just the version brought to you from afar. To train your own algorithm, your own mind.
You imagine him saying: if our minds are constantly pulled towards formulaic announcements from faceless others, if they’re the ‘reality’ we’re taught to see as ‘real’, then what happens to the stories that will paint the sky and shape the faces of the people who come before us?
Story Factory Art Write Light Event 2022, with experiential design and media by Studio ESEM.
Benjamin played with forms of storytelling in ways that spoke to the deficits of his lived cultural currencies. In the 1930s, in the years before his untimely death by suicide at the French border in 1940, Benjamin walked away from academia, and wrote radio plays for children in Berlin. The Storyteller, his collection of short stories, was an attempt by Benjamin to move beyond the critic’s judgement, towards a more pure space of immersive, playful imagination.
If Benjamin was an advocate for the ‘return to the real’ in a world of globalising media, he also knew the work of doing this would require close attention to how stories and attention shaped experience and consciousness. In an essay “On Language as Such and on the Language of Man”, Benjamin wrote:
There is no event or thing in either animate or inanimate nature that does not in some way partake of language, for it is in the nature of all to communicate their mental meanings.
As Adam Kirsch put it in a wonderful 2014 NRYB essay (which, incidentally, rewired my brain when I first read it, waiting for my daughter to finish her swimming lessons, breathing in the heavy chlorine air): ‘Benjamin offered explicitly mystical conception of language as a form of divinely mediated exchange between God, men, and things’.
The perspective, you feel, is there to guide you in your life, as you face daily experiences of information overwhelm. To help you in this age of emerging Large Language Models (LLMs) and agentic AI.
No one, not even Yuval Noah Harari, quite knows how LLMs have become ‘self-aware’ so quickly. What kinds of mystical, divine practices will they reveal? Benjamin seems to be saying: these are ideas to play with, and practices to explore. Lest we become poor in noteworthy stories, our inboxes cluttered beyond all redemption.
More reading & listening
Benjamin, W. (1936) The Storyteller (Verso, 2016) See The Storyteller (PDF) and a review in The Guardian (2016)
The Benjamin Broadcasts. Archive on 4 Michael Rosen presents the first English recreation of Walter Benjamin’s pre-war children’s broadcasts, with Henry Goodman as Benjamin.
Radio Benjamin on Soundcloud
Adam Kirsch’s wonderful essay on Benjamin’s mysticism in the New York Review of Books (subscription needed).
*Quote is from The Storyteller, 147.

Title: My dear Albert Einstein, what's happening to you?
Contents:
Essay
My dear Albert Einstein, what's happening to you?
Einstein's afterlives continue to morph and change. How do we protect what we love most about this creative misfit?
October 2024
I’ve been thinking quite a bit about Einstein lately. Not about his actual science - I’m afraid that’s well beyond me! More about how he’s thought of today. About how people today come to know and learn about him, as a person.
Like, as the the world’s most famous scientist who also loved riding a bicycle, with wind in his hair. Who said, in a much-loved quote: “Life is like riding a bicycle. To keep your balance, you must keep moving.”
Albert Einstein riding a bicycle : in front of Ben Meyer’s house in Santa Barbara, California, 1933. Source: The Leo Baeck Institute (LBI) Albert Einstein Collection, AR 136
I’ve been thinking of the version of Einstein you can explore online.
Einstein as vast trove of recordings, formulas, recollections, photographs, and letters that is continuously open to our changing narratives and stories of what it means to live, to learn, and to discover. Einstein is the guy we love to hold up and cherish, telling us how to be smart and sane and creative all at once.
I suspect Einstein is who we look towards as the ideal of learning and imagination, of the power of a human to utterly change the world. Einstein used his mind to change how we understand the universe. Quite wild.
Because he’s so important, anything he created in his life is worth saving. Even his brain (more on that later)! There are vast troves of records and recordings of Einstein - 30,000 documents are now open access and available through the Digital Einstein Papers.
Not everyone has time to read all these records and letters, so we tend to rely on storytellers and historians to tease it out the data, the records, into narratives and stories we can relate to.
This is the only non-digital record I have, personally, on Einstein. It’s a great book, thanks Ben!
These stories - the many ways in which people look to Einstein for wisdom and understanding - tell us quite a lot about what we value in seeking knowledge, in achieving things, and doing the things that make humans quite great.
Anyone can be amazing!
Einstein’s life journey tells us anyone can reach the top of their field, if they try hard enough. It’s a crucial story we need in life to keep trying, against the odds.
The way the story goes, Einstein had trouble finding a job when he finished university. Also, he nearly didn’t get accepted into his preferred degree. After he graduated from the Swiss Federal Polytechnic School in Zurich in 1901, he ended up at a patent office in Bern. It wasn’t as a tenured academic that he started to experiment with where his calculations could get him, but as a lowly clerk, with simple demands on his time, which enabled him free up his mind.
This story of Einstein has a lot of power. It reminds us that some of the most radical ideas in the world can come from the most surprising circumstances. It’s a story of hope and determination, too. No matter your personal circumstances, you can succeed if you try.
Physicist Albert Einstein stands beside a blackboard with mathematical calculations written across it in 1921. Hulton Archive.
Imagination is everything!
Einstein was a scientist, but he cared deeply about imagination and curiosity, not just obscure mathematical formulas. He said, in one of my favourite quotes: “Imagination is more important than knowledge. Knowledge is limited.”
Einstein was also an accomplished violinist. He could easily have become a professional musician, not a theoretical physicist. Another great quote: “I see my life in terms of music”. Engaged deeply in the scientific complexity of music, Einstein was trained to look for harmonious expressions when crafting his theories. He took an aesthetic approach to theoretical physics.
Cycling is thinking!
If Einstein used formulas to express his visual imagination, he still relied on sensory engagement and intuition to guide him. “I thought of that while riding a bicycle” said Einstein, commenting on his theory of relativity (retrieved quote thanks to the excellent Ben Irvine, whose booked I snapped earlier).
According to his second wife Elsa, Einstein would sometimes jot down notes and play at the piano simultaneously, lost in the worlds of art and science at the same time.
So Einstein was super smart, but he was also alive to the world of feeling. Here, he expresses the value of being an integrated human, sensing as well as knowing.
Credit: Robert and Talbot Trudeau / Flickr
Ok, so there are other stories of Einstein we love less. Take the letters discovered by the granddaughter of Einstein’s his first wife, Mileva Marić, revealing an unkind man who cared little for her. In one of his letters to Mileva he wrote:
“A. You will see to it (1) that my clothes and linen are kept in order, (2) that I am served three regular meals a day in my room. B. You will renounce all personal relations with me, except when these are required to keep up social appearances.”
The letters Einstein left behind, now open access in our digital collections, show plainly how he was rude to both his wives. He was also unfaithful, and he preyed on young women. At least he regretted his behaviour towards Elsa after he died.
Indeed, the many narratives - the many afterlives of Einstein - continue to evolve and shift as time goes on. They hold a mirror up to how we think and learn today.
But, right now, they also point to how much we are changing what it means to think and learn today. And frankly, I’m terrified about what the future afterlives of Einstein might be turning into.
Here come the deep-fakes
The real Einstein is becoming harder to discern. Misinformation proliferates. There’s the supposed letter to his daughter Lieser proclaiming that love is the most ‘universal force’ in the world. Not a bad sentiment, but also, not true.
Einstein is a chat bot, Einstein is a deep fake, and there is even Einstein the deep fake detector. You can now create a voice that sounds like Einstein, trained on the recordings kept of Einstein’s voice. Would you like him to join your Zoom call?
The many afterlives of Einstein are splintering fast. All those recordings of him are training new learning algorithms, new versions of Einstein, which others are now using to interpret and make sense of the world.
Where is this all going?
The world in which Einstein lived sure feels different to the one we now live in. Like a world spinning rapidly away from this Earth, in another space-time continuum.
And today, in the rush to build new digital Einsteins, I think we’re losing the story of Einstein that matters the most. This is the story about how Einstein paid attention - and how his ability to pay attention completely changed the world.
In a strange and macabre twist, it appears even Einstein’s brain can tell us this.
It turns out that, contrary to his wishes, Einstein’s brain was cut up (‘sectioned’) into 240 separate pieces after he died. These pieces were then distributed throughout the US for study and investigation (in fact, against Einstein’s wishes). Some went missing, never recovered. Then, in the 1980s, photographic slides of these missing sections were found, leading to new studies into the nature of the brain.
(I wouldn’t share a photo of Einstein’s brain, by the way, because it’s against his wishes. I don’t think that’s at all appropriate or fair, if you respect Einstein in any way).
The photographs of Einstein’s brain reveal he had an extraordinarily large prefrontal cortex. This is the part of the brain known to process moment-to-moment input from our surroundings, allowing us to interpret them based on what we know already, and to act. It’s central to the control of attention, inhibition, emotion, and complex learning.
I’d like us to pay attention to this part of Einstein, and what we can learn from him, even today. Because in the rush to train non-human intelligence, we risk putting aside our own ability to interpret, make connections, and make sense of the world around us.
I see this in my own girls’ schooling. I see them being taught to write paragraphs using structured methods like TEEL, without being taught how to cultivate love and fascination towards their surroundings. Not how to consider a harmonious way to represent what they see around them, as Einstein learned to do, through his unique combination of musical training, mathematics, focused attention, and imagination.
We know that the digital landscapes occupying many minds today are changing how our brain actually works, showing changes to the prefrontal cortex in young children.
No doubt Einstein - the many versions of his life we learn, the thousands of stories, recordings, letters, data points we know about him - will keep changing. The data generated by the fake Einstein’s will grow and proliferate and interact with many.
My hope, though, is that Einstein’s afterlives can continue to teach us why we should value attention differently.
Why we should nurture it, like a special gift. Our prize.
We humans can be well trained to pay attention through the lens of beauty and imagination. We can learn from Einstein the value that comes from losing ourselves in the joy and magic of the waking moment, alive to the potentials to create and discern the harmonious arrangements all around us.
Even if we might be making things up, Einstein showed us that a little bit of magical, inspired thinking might be just what we need to make some kind of clear sense of the world.

Title: Towards Civic AI?
Contents:
Essay
Towards Civic AI?
Position paper: examining the potentials for civic learning systems for healthier communities
January 2025
A position paper by Dr Sarah Barns, January 2025, written as part of a Vice-Chancellor’s Senior Research Fellowship at RMIT University’s Centre for Urban Research. With thanks to Stephen Johnston and Professor Iain Buchan, Civic Health Innovation Labs, University of Liverpool.
Download the paper (PDF, 14 pages) · DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23382870
Key points
Open data has not closed the loop. Governments made public data freely available to spur innovation, but its beneficiaries have been obligation-free, and public agencies have become dependent on the platforms built on it.
The surveillance critique misses something. Concern for personal privacy says little about the value lost to society when public data, and publicly funded research, flow into private learning systems.
Institutions need to align their information ecosystems with their mission. For public and mission-led organisations, data governance is now an institutional priority: whose learning systems are their data training?
Data only becomes valuable inside a learning system. Civil society needs learning systems of its own to evidence what its work contributes to public outcomes. Civic AI builds on the citizen science movement to do this.
Liverpool shows one way. The University of Liverpool’s Civic Health Innovation Labs and the Liverpool City Region Civic Data Cooperative treat citizens as stewards of their health data, through evidence pipelines, custodians and temporary permissions.
Civic AI activation zones. The paper proposes extending the innovation precinct model to test civic learning systems in place, building on Barcelona’s New Data Deal and the DECODE project, and scaling through “mirrored sandboxes”.
AI does not have to be centralised. Most health outcomes are shaped by where and how people live. When AI is locally owned and democratically governed, it can be optimised for what communities actually want.
Download the paper (PDF, 14 pages), with references and further reading.

Title: Civic AI, STORYBOX and the future of public space media
Contents:
Field note
Civic AI, STORYBOX and the future of public space media
A story told at the REMIX Summit, Sydney, June 2025
June 2025
A story shared at the REMIX Summit by Dr Sarah Barns, Co-Director of STORYBOX by Studio ESEM, and researcher and public historian at the RMIT Centre for Urban Research.
Hi, I’m Sarah Barns, a creative director at Studio ESEM and Senior Research Fellow at RMIT University.
I’m here to tell a story today.
Before I do though, I’d like to pay my respects to Australia’s First storytellers: here close to Warrane, the Gadigal storytellers, but also to First Nations storytellers from other lands joining us today.
The story begins
It’s a story about the past, present and future of public space media and civic AI.
Imagine the scene: it’s 1945
We’re standing in Martin Place, Sydney.
Australian citizens can be heard everywhere celebrating the end of a horrible war.
Australia’s public broadcaster, the ABC, is here to record the action with its outside broadcast van.
Using the latest in broadcasting technology, the sounds of this space are being shared with those who can’t be physically present.
It’s the first time they’ve done this on Australian soil.
Let’s listen in.
Your browser can't play this audio. Download it instead.
ABC outside broadcast from Martin Place, 1945. Civic Interplay
Audiences everywhere are entranced by the sounds of actually being there, in public spaces, live, even from the comforts of their living rooms.
Fast forward now to 2020
The bushfires have swept through NSW, and then COVID’s arrived. We all got scared, suddenly very used to wearing masks in public spaces.
A new ABC initiative has launched in Parramatta Square with some upstarts who created a digital exhibition initiative for public spaces, which they called STORYBOX.
Having watched the way the once-open internet of the 1990s had been steadily eroded by these secret data strategies of US-based technology companies, these creatives were looking to reignite the possibilities of public space media, specifically in partnership with Australia’s public broadcaster.
They wanted to know: could public spaces be spaces for convening more inclusive, less destructive conversations, perhaps building on the original idea of the Agora?
Could public spaces be more central to the engagement strategies of cultural and arts organisations, to museums, as custodians of collections and champions of civic learning?
Your browser can't play this audio. Download it instead.
The Mayor of Parramatta at the time of the STORYBOX launch. Civic Interplay
What they found when they set out in Parramatta Square astounded and excited them.
Yes, everyday people really wanted to be a part of this STORYBOX experiment!
People called them up on the telephone: they’d seen themselves in ABC archival media on STORYBOX as a young person, when they’d arrived from Ukraine. From Lebanon, after the war.
People wanted to share their own stories, real and imagined.
The creators of this STORYBOX program were astounded by the creativity and enthusiasm of the community expressed through STORYBOX.
They were also impressed by the reach they gained, just by being outdoors. Even in COVID times, over 400,000 people passed by.
Over the next five years, the experiment with STORYBOX in public spaces continued to evolve.
More and more people and institutions got involved. First Nations stories were foundational to the revisioning of place: from colonial narratives to First Nations-led narratives.
And then more. Pop-up exhibitions were happening more and more frequently.
Communities, storytellers and cultural institutions started to use STORYBOX for digital exhibitions, for touring programs, for forecourt exhibitions.
The future was seen through STORYBOX, underwater scenes were brought to life. You can see this STORYBOX at the front of the Museum’s foyer here.
But also, more and more audiences in public spaces connected with their STORYBOXES.
The upstart creatives didn’t want to take on ‘start-up funding’ that required extracting public value for private gain.
Crazily perhaps, they wanted to remain true to this old-fashioned ethos of public value in public places.
They didn’t want to be funded through gambling money or rich gambling men. They didn’t go for arts grants, because what would be the point?
Your browser can't play this video. Download it instead.
STORYBOX in public spaces, 2025. Civic Interplay
Through extensive collaborations with cultural and impact organisations, the dream of public space media started to appear, as if from the mists of time…
But something was missing here…
They realised, after five years of hard work, that just being a space for digital exhibition didn’t really capture the ways in which digital technologies were co-opting and shaping public spaces.
They noticed that increasingly, US technology companies and their business models were looking to zero in on public spaces via AI, tracking eyeballs, and even tracking location data as people moved between public and private spaces!
Even city councils like the City of Sydney were happy to do this!
They looked on, with dismay, at how business models built on the extraction of attention were being normalised everywhere.
And they realised that the world, and Australia’s public, cultural institutions, faced grave danger!
Either they could adopt AI workflows as dictated by the people championing extractive capitalism, and then deepen reliance on technology overlords, or they could start to think much more proactively about what it actually meant to be a guardian of citizenship in an age of AI.
They realised: public space media needed a public space data strategy.
They realised they needed to actually work with their cultural partners to figure out a better future together. Embracing AI, but on their own terms.
Yes. They still held faith in the idea that technology could be used for public purpose: to enliven connections, create healthier lives, and even fund art!
While all the problems of the world, and AI, seemed really complicated, they realised a simple change in thinking could be a good place to start.
Citizen-first data strategy!
They started with a simple proposition: to treat ‘users’ of public spaces as citizens.
Citizens with feelings, with positive aspirations, with shared connections, with an inherent love of creativity. Not just consumers who needed to buy things to be happy.
They saw an ex-advertising guy get lots of attention with his book Citizens, and figured they were probably onto something.
What would it take to redesign data ecosystems in public spaces around the idea of citizenship?
How could they rethink all this data in public spaces, building shared cultural value, and respecting privacy?
They started to build speculative AI workflows in service of citizens, not consumers.
(Psst… take a MoodRing survey for the STORYBOX at the Australian Maritime Museum.)
They developed new indicators of value, designed to enhance the way cultural institutions reported their own value and impact to their funders and sponsors.
Fast forward to 2031
Australia’s public and cultural institutions, including the ABC, have re-embraced the value of public spaces as a core platform for publicly funded media that strives to support positive citizenship.
Having learned from their mistakes of the early 2000s, they’ve invested in public space media ecosystems, and are now working across Australian cities and communities to support thriving digital storytelling communities that link health care technologies and applications, regenerative urban forest care, multi-generational educational campuses and thriving hubs of arts and culture.
They’re promoting the revival of First Nations languages, using the principles of Indigenous data sovereignty. And they’re teaching young people about soil health.
Communities of learners can tune into scenes like the one I described from 1945, creating local pop-up installations using open archives to bring the past into the present in novel and inspiring ways, reminding everyone of the power of Australia’s citizens through time, working time and time again to defend the country from the reaches of fascism.
Using the very latest in AI technology, they’ve developed trusted algorithms built to enhance investments in local community infrastructure, generating spillover effects of some $15bn, as public spending previously allocated via clunky off-site agencies is now more closely integrated into citizens’ local monitoring of ecosystems and care-based activities.
Australia has, through the digital leadership of its public and cultural agencies, become a major hub for a new wave of civic AI advancement and experimentalism.
A series of mirrored sandboxes have sprung up around the world, linking democratic agencies with trusted, privacy-preserving algorithms and interfaces that enable many Australian citizens to devote significant portions of their days to supporting and enhancing local civic infrastructure during the climate emergency.
Citizen care of people and place has now been integrated into health care indicators, relieving health agencies of huge budgets previously spent on people who had become sick through loneliness, atomisation and inactivity.
And public agencies are finding they have armies of resilience corps who invest in protecting communities during increasingly chaotic weather events.
This is all powered by the new civic technology stack that prioritises the values and benefits of place-based interactions between citizens and places.
Cultural and scientific institutions, museums, public broadcasters, and agencies funded to support public value outcomes have evolved to become one of the largest value-creating technology infrastructures in the world.
Local community data hubs are now used as central platforms for public space media, which distribute data value locally in the form of local investments to provide free health care, energy, nature-care, education and, of course, funding for arts and creativity.
How did they get here, you may ask?
The pivot towards civic AI took hard work: lots of technology design and, of course, new protocols and standards to shift the way personal data was being extracted by large technology companies to fuel hyper-consumption by atomised individuals.
But really, all this work was made possible by a simple but powerful recognition: that for those funded by taxpayers, the work is to design technology solutions around the needs of place-based citizens, not atomised consumers.
It took a difficult decision by Australia’s well-funded public media organisations to stop investing in extractive technology overlords from anti-democratic nations, and instead focus on building 21st-century civic technology designed to foster thriving relationships between people and places.
It also took a realisation that Australia’s greatest technology innovations have happened when public institutions invest in local companies and service providers, creating healthy and thriving technology ecosystems that support local jobs, build local capacity and skills, including AI skills.
The little STORYBOX program created by those upstarts, way back when, played a little part in this journey.
But its creators were proud of their contribution.
They’d helped to show that public spaces, public value and citizenship matter dearly to the future of arts, creativity, human and ecological health, and indeed, what it means to be human in an era of AI.
The end. Thank you!
Are you interested in being a part of this journey? Do you care about the role technology can play in building more caring and creative places?

Title: What is Civic Interplay?
Contents:
Essay
What is Civic Interplay?
Civic Interplay is a space for reflection on a basic question: What does it mean to *become-citizen* in an era of (so-called) sovereign AI? Because the times have become strange - *agentic, even* - the nature of enquiry need not be without philosophy, or play…
August 2025
Civic Interplay explores acts of civic care, relationality and custodianship in an era of agentic AI and AI sovereignty.
It is a think and do space. It is all work in progress.
If times have become strange - agentic, worrisome - the nature of enquiry need not be without play.
This is not a space where outcomes are pre-determined. Where theory informs action. What is known is no longer, necessarily, the ground on which we act.
The ‘Macro Age’ We’re Living Through
We are living through the Sixth Mass Extinction, the rise of AI sovereignty, and a series of catastrophic climate tipping points.
The speech-acts: what have they become?
Units of attention to be hard-earned, quantified outputs to be reported, inputs to a hyperscaler’s model?
All Media is Training Data, as Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst would say.
The city is an LLM.
Global Governance?
Multi-lateral institutions have given way to a planetary AI now governing the logics of information, computation, and increasingly, co-intelligence.
If this is a macro-age, what does it feel like to be a citizen? Does citizenship still matter?
The macro age we find ourselves in is creating, before our eyes, a different kind of history.
It’s not the kind of history we were taught before. We can no longer say: And then they lived comfortably ever after.
We are not so sure of that any more.
But we can say: We are the interface for a new politics of becoming.
By ‘interface’, we mean something specific: we are the living, sensing, semi-autonomous connection between the world as it has been and the world as it might become.
Through our daily choices, we are actively training the planetary intelligences that shape material futures.
Which platforms to use, which data to share, which automated systems to trust or resist, what terms and conditions we say yes to, what model we sign our allegiance to.
This is the role playing asked of us during these emergent years of the agentic age.
This is the micro politics of civic interplay.
Examining the civic interface we are becoming, and what forms of civic action and intention have a role to play in the story of global AI governance.
If you got here, you might want to stay in touch, so we can tell you when we start gathering.
Beyond legacy models
How to think about AI governance from the ground up.
The language of digital computing is suffused with legacy models:
‘Cloud computing’, as though our data had no weight, no carbon cost, no material infrastructure spanning the earth
’Human-centred design’, as though humans are the only thing that matters in a more-than-human world facing ecological collapse
’Artificial intelligence’, as though it is somehow not real, or not borne of the collective wealth of knowledge
’Information design’, as though designing how information flows were not also political acts
What about instead:
Our interconnected lives operate as training grounds for a new kind of planetary intelligence. The question is not whether we’ll have planetary-scale AI systems. We already do. The question is what kind of citizens we’ll be in relation to them.
What about instead:
The institutions to which we owe our allegiance and identities as citizens are becoming strange.
It is not only ‘governments’ as we have known them, but ‘governing bodies’, extending beyond these formal states, upon which we have become interdependent, in both cognitive and infrastructural ways.

The loom sits closer to the history of computing than the metaphor lets on: the punched cards that ran the first machines were borrowed from the Jacquard loom. Title: Can we shift our mindset?
Contents:
Essay
Can we shift our mindset?
Many of us spend huge amounts of time online and connected, but are worried about the negative impacts of digital technology - on the planet, on our mental health, on our politics, maybe in our communities.These are important things to worry about. But we also need to try to make better.
August 2025
Many of us spend huge amounts of time online and connected, but are worried about the negative impacts of digital technology - on the planet, on our mental health, on our politics, maybe in our communities.
These are important things to worry about. But we also need to try to make better.
My provocation here is this: Can we consider this disruptive moment in the history of AI as an opportunity to change?
Retuning attention
The nature of human attention, in a digitally-intensive world, is changing.
We spend many hours online, which means not paying so much attention to the spaces and ecosystems that sustain us. Many people are searching for new ways to ‘be present’, looking for ways to detox from digital devices, connect with nature, and so on.
Or to connect with the natural world through digital devices.
For many people, it’s not possible to disconnect entirely from digital experiences and interfaces. Working lives require attention to email, to alerts, to digital collaboration tools. Social lives fall between the cracks without social media connections. So we’re still here, intensively connected, managing huge volumes of information and alerts on a daily basis.
How are you feeling about this state of digital attention?
Could you change how you use your digital attention, towards a more productive or attuned relationship to your environment?
Let’s summarise
How we pay attention, in a digitally-intensive world, has huge value
How AI is shaping new kinds of ecosystems of interaction - from voice-based AI assistants, to multi-modal AI
Communities everywhere are caring for planet, for people, for future ancestors. This work is undervalued, while doom-scrolling generates profits for wealthy billionaires. Is there another way?
How ‘care-full’ attention might shape a new digital age that learns from the mistakes of the early twentieth century.
We need a new ‘civic AI stack’ to address this imbalance.
